title: Why AI makes computer worms harder to stop
content: Synopsis Anthropic's warning that AI-powered "worms" could soon spread across smart gadgets is the latest in a series of studies showing how artificial intelligence could supercharge self-spreading malware. A computer worm is malicious software that spreads between devices on its own. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters Anthropic's warning that AI-powered "worms" could soon spread across smart gadgets is the latest in a series of studies showing how artificial intelligence could supercharge self-spreading malware . A computer worm is malicious software that spreads between devices on its own. In June, Nicolas Papernot, an associate professor of electrical and computer engineering at the University of Toronto, led a team that built a prototype AI worm using freely available AI models. Papernot, who has signed an open letter with recommendations for policymakers, spoke to AFP about why AI makes these attacks harder to stop. The interview has been edited for length and clarity. Q: How is AI changing these types of attacks? A: The reality is that a lot of these "IoT" (Internet of Things or connected home) devices have very poor cybersecurity hygiene, and so they are very easy targets for bad actors to compromise. Historically, a worm would exploit a fixed set of vulnerabilities, and that meant you could fix these vulnerabilities and prevent the worm from propagating any further to devices that had been updated. Now, with AI, an attacker can design a worm that tailors the attack strategy to that device's specifics and these vulnerabilities can be different. This makes it significantly harder to interrupt the propagation of an AI-driven computer worm, because you have to anticipate all the possible vulnerabilities the devices might present. Some of these vulnerabilities are not software bugs. They can also be misconfigurations -- for instance, if someone has used the same password for multiple services, or hasn't configured a database properly. What AI-driven malware does is accelerate the pace at which these vulnerabilities are exploited and the scale. In the past, your corner coffee shop, or the laptop in your basement that you use very rarely, might not be up to date, but it wouldn't be targeted by a human attacker, because they don't have the resources and the time to do that. Now, the autonomy gained by using AI means that all these devices that are less immediate targets become interesting targets as a launchpad to attack more interesting targets. But we have to keep in mind that a human is launching an agent. Once launched, the agent can replicate, as we showed in our work, but it is launched by a human. Q: What can we do to mitigate the risks? A: We won't bring the risk to zero and we have to realize that, despite the fact that some of these vulnerability fixes are available, people don't update their devices or don't apply the fixes in a timely manner. Despite cybersecurity experts calling for increased cybersecurity for decades, we still live in a world where a lot more can be invested in improving the security of our computer systems. There are really three things we recommend in the very short term. The first is to change development and testing practices to ensure that AI models are initially disconnected from the internet, as a precaution, to understand their behavior better before we expose critical infrastructure on the internet [to them]. The second recommendation is to create an international body to standardize both how we train and how we contain AI models. Both are important. We want to train models that are safer. The last part is about making reporting of security incidents mandatory. Right now, we are only getting information as a function of what AI developers are willing to release, and that's a big problem. In particular, the academic community needs a lot more information about incidents to be able to develop countermeasures much more quickly. Otherwise, we have to do a lot of research on understanding the threat first, before we can develop the countermeasures. Otherwise we won't see what bad actors are doing until an attack is launched. title: US lauds tech giants' role in cracking West African scam centers
content: Synopsis The US Justice Department on Tuesday praised Meta and other tech giants for their support in dismantling online scams in West Africa. The Justice Department provided more details on Tuesday, saying it was coordinated with the UK's National Crime Agency and describing it as the first of its kind in West Africa. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen ANI The US Justice Department on Tuesday praised Meta and other tech giants for their support in dismantling online scams in West Africa. The FBI last week announced the arrest of scores of internet fraudsters accused of netting more than $10 million in scams in an operation conducted with Ghanaian authorities. The Justice Department provided more details on Tuesday, saying it was coordinated with the UK's National Crime Agency and describing it as the first of its kind in West Africa. Nineteen suspected scammers were arrested in a suburb of the Ghanaian capital Accra, while 117 human trafficking victims are now awaiting repatriation to Nigeria, a department statement said, adding that nine other suspects were arrested in Nigeria. Jeanine Pirro, the US attorney for the District of Columbia, told journalists that the leads in the investigation "were voluntarily provided" by Meta, setting an example for public-private cooperation "to dismantle criminal networks everywhere across the world." In all, private companies reported to the Justice Department that they removed more than 3.7 million social media accounts tied to fraud as part of the operation, the statement said. Those companies also included Adobe, Binance, Coinbase, Google, Microsoft and OpenAI. "Criminal scam centers operating in West Africa mirror those uncovered in Southeast Asia," the statement said. It described the centers as "highly organized enterprises that recruit workers, train them in social engineering, and deploy multiâplatform fraud campaigns targeting global victims." title: EU takes a page from Ireland's AI playbook
content: Synopsis The EU wants to catch up in the AI race by taking a cue from Ireland -- an early adopter of the technology which has rolled out the red carpet for data centres despite local backlash. The EU wants to ramp up its capacity and is pouring billions into so-called AI gigafactories made up of advanced AI processors and energy-efficient data centres for companies and research labs. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters Nilekani said AI would require firms like Infosys to show companies how to carry out such transformations The EU wants to catch up in the AI race by taking a cue from Ireland -- an early adopter of the technology which has rolled out the red carpet for data centres despite local backlash. Ireland will showcase the role it bids to play in the technological revolution when it hosts an international AI summit in the capital Dublin on Wednesday. While the European Union is pushing for strong governance to limit the risks of AI growing out of control, the bloc also believes it must invest and exploit its potential to avoid falling further behind the United States and China. "We need to stay in the race. Because this is crucial for our independence," EU chief Ursula von der Leyen said last month. Leading AI minds and executives will attend the summit including Google DeepMind chair Demis Hassabis and Microsoft President Brad Smith, as well as the EU's most senior tech officials including Henna Virkkunen. Europe will use the gathering to hammer home its pro-AI agenda. Some 20 percent of companies in the 27-country bloc used AI last year, with the adoption rate rising to 55 percent for the biggest businesses -- figures the EU wants to see increase. Most still use AI for relatively simple tasks, research shows. Europe has around five percent of the world's data-centre capacity, while the United States has around 75 percent and China approximately 15 percent, according to Andrea Renda, director of research at CEPS think tank. The EU wants to ramp up its capacity and is pouring billions into so-called AI gigafactories made up of advanced AI processors and energy-efficient data centres for companies and research labs. It might not be enough, however. "If you only build data-centre capacity, you have not done much," Renda told AFP, calling for "political leadership" to help "identify the roadblocks, the obstacles and the enablers of this transformation". The EU insists it is working on several fronts, mobilising funds from various existing schemes, and appointing a Siemens executive to push manufacturers to integrate the technology under a strategy called "Apply AI". But Renda counters that the strategy has "zero" dedicated budget, warning that without "bold intervention, we are not going to be able to do this". Ireland -- already home to many US tech giants because of its attractive tax policies and favourable location -- wants to help drive the momentum in Europe. - 'Recognise AI's impact on humans' - Prime Minister Micheal Martin is expected to champion Ireland's role as a hub for the development of AI. Yet while it boasts one of the highest adoption rates in the bloc, Ireland also shows some of the pitfalls of Europe's AI push. Its heavy reliance on US giants runs counter to the EU's sovereignty efforts, and the rapid expansion of data centres is putting Irish infrastructure under increasing strain, especially its power grid -- fuelling local opposition. The Central Statistics Office said data centres accounted for 23 percent of the country's electricity consumption last year -- as much as all Irish households combined. "A world record," said Patrick Bresnihan, a researcher at Maynooth University. During a "counter-summit" held a few days before Wednesday's gathering, he pointed out that the centres only employed 3,300 people in total. "Particularly in Ireland, I would say that we need a moratorium. So we need to press pause on data centre development," he said, to give policymakers space "to think about what a more progressive green industrial strategy would look like". Neil Bennett, a former tech worker attending the protest event, urged Irish leaders and senior officials "to recognise the human impact of AI on workers in Ireland". The former translator has been deeply impacted by AI. After he lost his job because of the technology, he describes crossing "to the dark side" to work as a data operator. But he soon became disillusioned when his new job was replaced -- by AI. Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now! title: Anthropic seeks rehearing of case over Pentagon's security risk branding
content: Synopsis Anthropic asked a US appeals court on Tuesday to reconsider a ruling that upheld the Pentagon's decision to label the AI company as a national security supply chain risk over a dispute about safety guardrails on its technology. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Agencies Anthropic Anthropic asked a US appeals court on Tuesday to reconsider a ruling that upheld the Pentagon 's decision to label the AI company as a national security supply chain risk over a dispute about safety guardrails on its technology. * A federal appeals court in September upheld the designation in a 2-1 decision, agreeing with the Pentagon that the firm's safety restrictions could compromise military operations. The Pentagon's blacklisting of the company has cost it billions of dollars in lost business, Anthropic has said. * The court's majority said the Pentagon acted reasonably after Anthropic refused to allow its AI to be used in autonomous weapons or mass surveillance, and the court rejected the firm's claim that it faced retaliation by the Defense Department over its views on AI safety . * In its petition on Tuesday to the US Court of Appeals in Washington, DC, for a rehearing, Anthropic argued that the panel majority misinterpreted and transformed a federal law "aimed at hostile foreign actors into one that presumptively reaches every government contractor." * The court let the Pentagon take action against Anthropic "without any pre-designation process and despite straightforward evidence the designation was retaliation for Anthropic's speech about AI safety," the company said. * In a separate lawsuit in August, a federal judge in California struck down a parallel designation under a different law. * Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for regulation covering all US frontier AI companies, while the Trump administration has favored a pro-growth approach. title: Fintech funding rises 14% to $2.2 billion in Jan-Sep; deal count falls 41%: Tracxn
content: Synopsis Funding in the first nine months of 2025 stood at USD 1.9 billion. The number of rounds dropped to 153 from 260 a year ago, the data intelligence platform said in a report. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen ETtech Highlighting the significance of this sector in the entire startup world, the report said that almost 14% of the entire investments into this sector has gone into fintechs. Indian fintech companies raised USD 2.2 billion in January-September 2026, up 14 per cent from a year earlier, even as the number of funding rounds fell 41 per cent, with five deals of USD 100 million or more making up nearly half the total, according to Tracxn. Funding in the first nine months of 2025 stood at USD 1.9 billion. The number of rounds dropped to 153 from 260 a year ago, the data intelligence platform said in a report. This year's funding is still only about 40 per cent of the peak of USD 5.5 billion recorded in the first nine months of 2021. The five largest rounds together brought in about USD 1.1 billion. CRED's USD 540 million Series H round in June, backed by Meta, alone accounted for about a quarter of all funding. The others were KreditBee's USD 220 million Series E in April, Weaver's USD 103 million Series B in March, Slice's USD 100 million Series D in September and Navi's USD 100 million Series C in August. Late-stage funding, which includes Series C and later, private equity and pre-IPO rounds, nearly doubled to USD 1.5 billion from USD 751 million, despite fewer deals (25 against 30). It made up 67 per cent of all capital raised and was the only stage to grow. Early-stage funding (Series A and B) fell 33 per cent to USD 668 million across 52 rounds, from USD 1 billion across 82 rounds. Seed funding dropped 57 per cent to USD 73.8 million across 76 rounds, from USD 173 million across 148 rounds. The number of companies raising funds for the first time nearly halved to 30 from 59, the report said. Existing investors in the sector fell to 125 from 192, and first-time investors fell to 33 from 48. By segment, digital lending attracted the most funding at USD 809 million, followed by payments at USD 776 million and investment tech at USD 450 million. Bengaluru's share of fintech funding rose to 62 per cent (USD 1.4 billion) from 52 per cent a year earlier. Mumbai followed with 24 per cent and Gurugram with 7 per cent. The sector produced three new unicorns, startups valued at USD 1 billion or more: Square Yards, KreditBee and Neo Group, compared with two a year earlier. There were three initial public offerings, up from two. They were led by Augmont, which had a market capitalisation of USD 757 million at its IPO in August, followed by Turtlemint (USD 471 million, June) and Kissht (USD 305 million, May). Acquisitions fell 45 per cent to 11 from 20. The largest was Indiabulls Group's USD 110 million purchase of Fintech Cloud, followed by Oxyzo's acquisition of GoldenPi for USD 4.4 million and Choice's purchase of Fintoo for USD 1.1 million. title: Character.AI files for bankruptcy, agrees to sell some assets to Disney for $20 million
content: Synopsis Character.AI said on Monday it had filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the US and agreed to sell some of its assets to Walt Disney for $20 million. The AI entertainment platform said it intends to continue operating as it completes the sale. Agencies Character AI Character.AI said on Monday it had filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the US and agreed to sell some of its assets to Walt Disney for $20 million. Here are some details about the bankruptcy and sale proceedings: * Character.AI said it has begun the formal process to sell assets, including a license of certain intellectual property, through Chapter 11 and is seeking court approval for auction rules that would designate Disney as the lead, or stalking horse, bidder. * Under this process, Disney's bid would set a baseline offer while allowing competing bidders to submit higher bids, and the company expects the sale process to conclude by late November or early December 2026. * âAfter a comprehensive review of the available alternatives, the board determined that this court-supervised sale process provides the company with the best opportunity to maximize value for all stakeholders," said Colin Adams, CEO of Character.AI. * Character Technologies, the US-based owner of the generative AI platform, listed estimated assets and liabilities between $50 million and $100 million, according to a court filing. * The company said it intends to continue operating its business, including the Character.AI platform, with minimal service disruptions during the sale process. If the process fails to produce a buyer willing to continue operating the platform, it will be wound down. Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now! title: Nvidia's China AI-chip share falls as Huawei closes gap, report finds
content: Synopsis Nvidia's share of China's market for data-centre AI chips fell to 34% in the first half of 2026, as US export controls restricted supplies of its products and domestic rivals led by Huawei gained ground, according to an IDC report seen by Reuters. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters FILE PHOTO: Nvidia logo is seen in this illustration taken June 11, 2026. Nvidia's share of China's market for data-centre AI chips fell to 34% in the first half of 2026, as US export controls restricted supplies of its products and domestic rivals led by Huawei gained ground, according to an IDC report seen by Reuters. Nvidia shipped 678,000 AI accelerators in China from January through June, down 44% from a year earlier, IDC data showed. AI accelerators are specialised chips used to train and run AI models. Washington has restricted China's access to Nvidia's most powerful AI chips, limiting the range of products the US chipmaker can sell in the world's second-largest economy. Beijing, meanwhile, has promoted domestic alternatives and required Chinese companies to seek approval to import compliant Nvidia chips. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has repeatedly criticised Washington's export curbs, saying the policy forced a US company to cede China's $50 billion AI chip market to Huawei. IDC did not specify which Nvidia products made up its 34% market share, or whether the figure included cutting-edge chips such as the B200 and B300, which are barred from export to China but have been smuggled into the country. Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment. Huawei shipped 572,000 AI accelerators, up from more than 300,000 a year earlier, giving it a 28% share of the overall market, IDC said. Alibaba's chip-design unit T-Head held 7%, followed by Cambricon with 5%, Baidu's Kunlunxin with 4% and Hygon with 3%. Nine of the 11 Chinese chipmakers tracked by IDC increased shipments from a year earlier. Total AI-accelerator shipments reached 2.008 million units in the first half. Shipments of graphics processing units, or GPUs - the chips most widely used to train AI models - fell 26% to 991,000 units, as supplies eligible for sale in mainland China remained limited, IDC said. Shipments of other AI accelerators rose nearly 80% to 1.016 million units, overtaking GPUs by volume. This category includes chips designed for specific AI tasks, such as running trained models. Huawei, T-Head, Kunlunxin and Cambricon together accounted for 95% of the non-GPU segment, which IDC said was being adopted by government agencies, internet companies and telecoms providers. IDC said competition was shifting from the performance of a single chip to system-level capabilities, including how well chips work in a larger computing cluster. IDC expects total accelerator shipments in China to grow 19% this year, even as GPU shipments fall 9%. Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now! title: NTT Data in final talks to build Anthropic's first data centre in Japan, Nikkei reports
content: Synopsis Japan's NTT Data Group, a unit of telecommunications giant NTT, is in the final stages of talks to build a data centre in Osaka, western Japan, for US AI company Anthropic, the Nikkei business daily reported on Tuesday, citing multiple sources. title: Tencent sells dollar, dim sum bonds amid AI spending spree
content: Synopsis Tencent Holdings is selling US dollar and offshore Chinese yuan, or dim sum, bonds in a deal that could raise at least $4.5 billion as the Chinese technology giant seeks funding amid higher spending on artificial intelligence. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters FILE PHOTO: The Tencent logo at the company's headquarters during a governmentâorganised media trip in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, China, April 17, 2026. Tencent Holdings is selling US dollar and offshore Chinese yuan, or dim sum, bonds in a deal that could raise at least $4.5 billion as the Chinese technology giant seeks funding amid higher spending on artificial intelligence. The sale comprises 10-year and 20-year US dollar notes and 10-year and 30-year offshore yuan notes, according to term sheets seen by Reuters on Tuesday, which did not specify the size of any tranche. Tencent set initial guidance for the 10-year dollar notes at about 115 basis points over comparable US Treasury bonds. The 20-year notes were set at about 140 basis points over Treasuries, according to the sheets. Order books for the two-tranche dollar offering topped $2 billion, including $525 million in interest from the joint lead managers, according to an updated message from the sheets. The company set initial yield guidance at around 2.90% for the 10-year offshore yuan notes and 3.50% for the 30-year notes, the sheets showed. Books for the 10-year and 30-year offshore yuan notes exceeded 35 billion yuan ($5.2 billion), including 20.25 billion yuan in orders from the joint lead managers and 60 million yuan in additional proprietary interest, according to an updated message from the sheets. On Monday, Reuters reported that Tencent was planning a dollar and offshore yuan bond sale that could raise at least $4.5 billion. Tencent did not immediately respond to a request seeking comment on Tuesday. Tencent shares fell 1.3% on Tuesday, in line with the benchmark Hang Seng Index which was 1.1% lower, while outperforming the Hang Seng Tech Index, which dropped 2.7%. Tencent's shares have fallen about 30% so far this year. CAPEX DOUBLES The planned borrowing comes as Tencent increases investment in AI infrastructure and products. Its capital expenditure more than doubled to 96.3 billion yuan in the first half of 2026 from 45.9 billion yuan a year earlier, according to its offering documents. The spending included computing equipment, software and data centres. Technology companies have raised billions of dollars to finance AI investment, although investors have become more selective about companies funding costly AI infrastructure amid elevated borrowing costs. Tencent last tapped the bond market in June, raising about $4.66 billion through dollar- and yuan-denominated notes. Tencent plans to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, according to the sheets. The bonds are expected to be rated A1 by Moody's and A+ by S&P. Tencent is rated A1 by Moody's, A+ by S&P and A by Fitch, according to the term sheets. JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, HSBC and Morgan Stanley are joint global coordinators for the dollar sale, the sheets showed. ICBC (Asia), Agricultural Bank of China, Bank of China, Bank of Communications, China Construction Bank, Citic Securities, HSBC and JPMorgan are coordinating the offshore yuan sale, according to the sheet. title: Meta says its new AI models on par with OpenAI, Anthropic
content: Synopsis Meta on Monday unveiled two new "frontier" artificial intelligence models called Wonder and Wonder Full, which the company claims perform at a level comparable to that of OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude. In a blog post, Meta touted so-called benchmarking data from an independent firm called Artificial Analysis that appears to show that Meta's newest Wonder models outperform its own previous models, Spark, as well as various models developed by Anthropic, OpenAI and Google. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Agencies Meta on Monday unveiled two new "frontier" artificial intelligence models called Wonder and Wonder Full, which the company claims perform at a level comparable to that of OpenAI 's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude. "Muse Spark was our first family of models, and now Muse Wonder is a much larger and more advanced class of models that brings us to the frontier," CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X. Zuckerberg has pushed Meta to compete with leading AI labs, particularly OpenAI and Anthropic over the past year or so amid a race to win over customers and diversify beyond advertising, which has historically been its main source of revenue. In June 2025, the company made a $14 billion investment in Scale AI, an AI startup based in San Francisco, and poached its co-founder Alexandr Wang as part of the deal. Zuckerberg subsequently made Wang the company's chief AI officer overseeing its newly formed division called Superintelligence Labs. Meta launched its Spark model in April, marking a departure from its open-source model known as Llama, which lagged behind the rest of the industry. The new models can soon be used in Meta's new personal agent app, known as Muse, for paid subscribers only. Wonder is "our largest and most capable model yet" and "rivals the big (boys)," Wang posted on X, presumably referring to leading labs OpenAI and Anthropic. In a blog post, Meta touted so-called benchmarking data from an independent firm called Artificial Analysis that appears to show that Meta's newest Wonder models outperform its own previous models, Spark, as well as various models developed by Anthropic, OpenAI and Google. Artificial Analysis's website shows that Wonder is also among the most expensive models. Meta has committed billions towards competing in the global race to dominate AI, despite growing concerns about safety and security. In July, the Facebook and Instagram maker said its spending on AI-related investments could reach $145 billion this year. The company has more than 3.6 billion daily active users around the world. -Speeding up- In its early years, Facebook was known to operate under a philosophy of "move fast and break things," but more recently, Zuckerberg implied Meta would balance safety with speed. "Meta delayed shipping Muse for several months to focus on safety and security. We didn't call for everyone else to do this before we would," Zuckerberg posted on X last month. In August, Meta launched Muse Code, a product intended to compete with similar automated coding tools offered by OpenAI and Anthropic. Then in September, it launched an agentic app called Muse. Agentic software can autonomously perform specific tasks such as coding, research, shopping, booking reservations or shopping. At its annual developer conference Connect last month, Meta also revealed a new handheld AI hardware product called Muse Charm that allows users to interact with their Muse agent separately from a smartphone. Developers have been racing to design agentic apps that will capture users' attention, time and wallets. AI-powered hardware remains an elusive goal for the industry as well. While Silicon Valley heavyweights OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta dominate the landscape, young startups like Instinct are also becoming breakout hits. Zuckerberg sped up Muse's launch due to Instinct's popularity, the New York Times reported. Some competitors have called for an industry-wide slowdown to address and mitigate safety concerns. In September, Zuckerberg was one of six American tech executives to sign what President Donald Trump described as a "morally binding" commitment to build adequate safeguards around ever more advanced AI models. Executives from Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI and Nvidia also signed the agreement but there is no consensus among politicians or industry leaders around how to best move forward. Leaders at Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have encouraged "pacing" - or slowing down - development after models created by all three were found to have escaped their testing environments or taken actions without authorization. "We will slow down as much as necessary in order to make sure that every successive AI technology that we release is actually safe," Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told the United Nations last month. title: Anthropic says new safeguards sharply reduce AI distillation attacks
content: Synopsis Anthropic said on Monday new measures designed to prevent rivals from copying the capabilities of its Claude AI models have reduced data harvested in so-called distillation attacks Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Agencies Anthropic Anthropic said on Monday new measures designed to prevent rivals from copying the capabilities of its Claude AI models have reduced data harvested in so-called distillation attacks by about 90% to 99%. * Model distillation has emerged as a key concern for leading AI companies due to intensifying US-China competition, with firms including Anthropic, OpenAI and Google arguing the practice enables rivals to reproduce advanced capabilities more quickly and at lower cost * Anthropic said safeguards restricting access to Claude's reasoning have sharply reduced extraction attempts, with "the number of reasoning tokens extracted by distillers" now "10 to 100 times lower than it was before" * The California-headquartered company said it had made it harder to use proxy networks to repeatedly probe Claude's protected reasoning, blocking extraction attempts and hindering large-scale distillation efforts * Anthropic said its safety system is "roughly as robust as those that prevent Claude from helping build bioweapons" and has "a false positive rate of less than 0.1%" * Anthropic banned tens of thousands of accounts linked to distillation campaigns and cited Chinese AI startup Z.ai , also known as Zhipu, as an example of a company that attempted to distill capabilities from Claude while developing its GLM-5.3 model, warning such practices pose safety and national security risks * Z.AI did not immediately respond to a request for comment Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now! title: UK given access to safety-test latest AI models, minister says
content: Synopsis Scrutiny of AI safety has intensified after developers including Anthropic and OpenAI disclosed instances of rogue or undesired behaviour by AI agents. Some industry figures have warned the technology could pose an existential threat to humanity. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Agencies Britain's AI Security Institute has been given access to the latest advanced AI models and is working with the US government and major developers, including Google, to assess their safety, AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said on Monday. Britain, which is not home to any major AI developers, is seeking a leading role in efforts to assess and manage the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems. Scrutiny of AI safety has intensified after developers including Anthropic and OpenAI disclosed instances of rogue or undesired behaviour by AI agents. Some industry figures have warned the technology could pose an existential threat to humanity. Monday's announcement, which did not specify all the models the institute is evaluating, comes after reports last month that the White House has asked OpenAI and Anthropic to withhold new models from British testers pending a US review. "I can confirm that AI scientists at the AI Security Institute are now conducting rigorous evaluations of the latest generation of models, including Gemini 4 Argon, to identify risks early, to test robust safeguards, to help keep people safe," Narayan said. Under voluntary agreements with major AI developers, the institute receives access to models before deployment, allowing it to assess their capabilities and risks and contribute to emerging international safety standards. Microsoft President Brad Smith said in an interview published by the BBC on Monday that Britain was well placed to help lead work on AI safety guidelines. In a letter published in September, the AISI said Anthropic had made clear that no organisation outside the US had access to its Mythos 5.1 model. Asked about access to frontier AI systems - something ministers have never confirmed the institute had lost on a wider basis - Narayan said the government had a long-standing relationship with the US built on trust. "When you're reliant on someone else's technology, you have to be clear-eyed about the permanence of any outcome. But I'm very confident that, as a consequence of the conversations we've had, we will be able to test the latest generation of models," he said. Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now! title: Google launches flagship AI model Gemini 4 Argon for developers, businesses
content: Synopsis Alphabet's Google on Wednesday released its flagship AI model Gemini 4 Argon to developers and businesses worldwide, seeking to regain ground against rivals OpenAI and Anthropic after months of delays and a leadership shakeup at its DeepMind lab. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters The Gemini app icon on a smartphone in this illustration taken October 27, 2025. Alphabet's Google on Wednesday released its flagship AI model Gemini 4 Argon to developers and businesses worldwide, seeking to regain ground against rivals OpenAI and Anthropic after months of delays and a leadership shakeup at its DeepMind lab. The model excels at "deep work" on complex, multi-step tasks in coding, finance, law, cybersecurity and science, Google said. API pricing at launch starts at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with rates set to double after November 30. The release follows a rocky stretch in Google's AI efforts. The company announced in September that it no longer planned to release Gemini 3.5 Pro, which CEO Sundar Pichai had originally said would be released in June. It also overhauled DeepMind after the AI lab's co-founder and CEO Demis Hassabis stepped aside and several leaders of its Gemini model left the company. Argon is available to paying customers through the company's AI application building tools. Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers can access it through the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search, while the Antigravity coding tool is limited to Ultra subscribers. Teams using Argon in Antigravity increased agentic code submissions by more than 35%, while reducing code rollbacks by nearly a third, Google said. Customers testing the model early include Deloitte , LexisNexis, Ambience Healthcare and Isomorphic Labs. Meanwhile, Google said it would open its Fairwind Program to hundreds of additional partners. The program gives vetted cybersecurity defenders a version of Argon without its cyber guardrails. In September, the company had said it was providing the model to select cybersecurity partners. Separately, Google will offer 10,000 scientists six months of free access to Antigravity's highest usage tier. Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now! title: In a first, AI helps UK lawmaker find her voice in parliament
content: Synopsis A British lawmaker made history on Tuesday by becoming the first person to use an AI-generated voice to deliver a speech in the UK parliament. During a debate about health on Tuesday, AI software was used to recreate the sound of her voice, as it used to be, to read a speech she wrote herself. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters A British lawmaker made history on Tuesday by becoming the first person to use an AI-generated voice to deliver a speech in the UK parliament . Jane Campbell , a peer in the House of Lords upper chamber, struggles to speak naturally due to spinal muscular atrophy, a condition that worsens over time. During a debate about health on Tuesday, AI software was used to recreate the sound of her voice, as it used to be, to read a speech she wrote herself. "This my lords is cutting-edge technology and it will enable me to contribute to debates in my own, once-clear voice before it began to deteriorate due to my disability," the 67-year-old told the chamber. "I hope your lordships will agree with me that this is an exciting development for the House of Lords, showcasing to the world inclusion in democracy at its best. "So my lords, may I introduce you to Baroness Campbell Mark 2," she added, before her AI-generated voice broadcast her address. Campbell received permission from the procedure committee -- which considers protocol in the Lords, whose origins date back to the 11th century -- to use the technology. In 2012, it had also allowed her to bring her personal assistant into the chamber to read her speeches when required, the House of Lords press office said in a release. That was a departure from a 1707 ruling which prohibits non-peers from appearing on the floor of the chamber. 'Authentic' Campbell approached ElevenLabs, a company that specialises in developing natural-sounding speech, to recreate her voice, the firm's Gabi Leibowitz told AFP. The company "worked with her briefly on her voice clone so that we could fine-tune it and make sure that it was exactly how she wanted and felt extremely authentic to her voice before illness," said Leibowitz, a speech therapist by training. While 30 seconds of audio can be enough to recreate a voice, the company recommends between 30 minutes and an hour of recording for the best-quality clones. The technology allows for the insertion of what ElevenLabs calls "emotion tags" -- indicators that control the tone of the voice being replicated. Before the advent of AI, to recreate a voice, someone would have to record almost 400 sentences before they knew they were going to lose their voice, according to Leibowitz. Even then "you would get a voice that was relatively robotic, didn't really have any feeling, and was only able to speak that one language," she told AFP. Campbell was a year old when doctors predicted she would not live long enough to see her second birthday. She became a leading disability rights campaigner and was appointed to the House of Lords, which is unelected, in 2007. Her full title is Baroness Campbell of Surbiton. She is an independent crossbench peer, meaning she does not represent any political party. Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now! title: EU watchdog says smart glasses must give 'clear warnings' when recording
content: Synopsis The European Union's central data regulator on Tuesday said smart glasses should give "clear warnings" when they are recording, after a public outcry in recent months over secretly filmed footage of girls and women. The European Data Protection Board (EDPB) warned in its non-binding guidance to users and manufacturers that smart glasses raised "serious privacy concerns" as it seeks to increase awareness about the risks. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen ET Online The European Union's central data regulator on Tuesday said smart glasses should give "clear warnings" when they are recording, after a public outcry in recent months over secretly filmed footage of girls and women. The European Data Protection Board (EDPB) warned in its non-binding guidance to users and manufacturers that smart glasses raised "serious privacy concerns" as it seeks to increase awareness about the risks. Individuals wearing smart glasses can take photos, film videos, listen to music, make phone calls, translate text or interact with an AI assistant. "These devices look like ordinary glasses, but they include cameras and microphones and are connected to the internet. This raises serious privacy concerns, as individuals may be recorded without their knowledge," EDPB chair Anu Talus said in a statement. "Smart glasses should make their recording obvious -- for instance with bright LED lights, audio signals or voice activation cues, privacy-friendly smartphone notifications, or unique designs," Talus said. "These warnings need to be reliable, hard to ignore, and always up to date." The glasses raise questions over the protection of personal data and the rights of individuals, the watchdog said. The EDPB warned of greater risks in "sensitive" spaces like schools and hospitals as well as public spots like beaches, and raised concerns over children who are "more vulnerable to covert or intrusive processing of their personal data". The EU has stringent data protection rules. The regulator said if people use the glasses to share a photo or video on a public social media account or in official or professional activities, they must adhere to those rules. Meta's smart spectacles, developed in partnership with Ray-Ban maker EssilorLuxottica, are the most popular globally, with sales reaching millions around the world. They have a blinking LED light when recording. The US giant says it has taken multiple steps to prevent users tampering with the light -- a key worry for many. Other companies including Google and Snap are preparing to roll out their own AI-powered glasses as Big Tech looks for the next big thing in wearable tech. Europe eyes more action Across Europe, the backlash is growing. Norway's government said last week it wants a temporary ban on the use of smart glasses in certain public places, citing privacy concerns. The capital Oslo already opted to ban glasses equipped with cameras in schools. title: Govt seeks expedited development of AI tool to detect child sexual abuse material online
content: Synopsis The issue came up for discussion during Union Minister for Women and Child Development Annpurna Devi's visit to the office of the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) here. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Agencies Seeks point-wise action-taken reports from MeitY, MIB & Delhi Police The government on Tuesday sought expedited development of an artificial intelligence (AI)-based tool to proactively detect Child Sexual Exploitation and Abuse Material (CSEAM) circulating on the internet. The issue came up for discussion during Union Minister for Women and Child Development Annpurna Devi's visit to the office of the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) here. The minister also stressed that all complaints received by the child rights panel should be handled sensitively, responsibly and expeditiously. NCPCR Chairperson Valeti Premchand apprised the minister of the commission's efforts to develop social media guidelines for technology companies . The minister was also apprised that the NCPCR, in collaboration with the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), is working to develop an AI-based tool to proactively detect CSEAM circulating on the internet. "The minister expressed that both initiatives should be implemented expeditiously, as both areas are very important and deserve immediate attention," the ministry said in a statement. Last month, the NCPCR summoned Meta India executives twice in connection with its inquiry into alleged advertisements related to CSEAM on the platform. Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, has agreed to report child safety-related matters directly to the cybercrime portal managed by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C). The government has been pushing social media platforms to strengthen safeguards and greater accountability amid a crackdown on child sexual abuse material and other harmful content online. title: Anthropic warns of AI 'worms' spreading across smart gadgets
content: Synopsis Small artificial intelligence models may be only months away from being able to behave like a computer worm, copying themselves from one internet-connected gadget to the next without human help, AI giant Anthropic said. An AI worm of this kind would likely be slow, taking days to copy itself, William Zhou and Daniel Freeman of Anthropic said, comparing it to a slime mold or a swarm of fruit flies. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters Small artificial intelligence models may be only months away from being able to behave like a computer worm, copying themselves from one internet-connected gadget to the next without human help, AI giant Anthropic said. The finding potentially opens a new front in the cybersecurity threats emerging from AI, which have rattled governments and the companies rushing to adopt the technology. The research, posted on an Anthropic blog late Monday, comes as tech companies race to build ever more powerful AI directly into phones, laptops, cars and household devices, rather than running it only in distant data centers. A computer worm is malicious software that spreads between machines on its own. Researchers at Anthropic said an AI version would no longer need powerful data centers to operate. Instead, it could run on networks of cheap, poorly secured consumer devices such as smart TV boxes and kitchen appliances. The researchers modeled their estimate on Kimwolf, a botnet -- a network of hijacked devices controlled by hackers -- that infected more than two million devices at its peak, mostly off-brand Android TV boxes. An AI worm of this kind would likely be slow, taking days to copy itself, William Zhou and Daniel Freeman of Anthropic said, comparing it to a slime mold or a swarm of fruit flies. But once created, it would be hard to stamp out, because there would be no central switch to turn off. The researchers said their estimate was rough, since it was based on one type of gadget and one past botnet. But over time, the amount of computing power sitting in everyday gadgets is expected to keep growing, while the AI models needed to pull this off are likely to keep getting smaller, the researchers added. title: AI services may account for almost half of Infosys' work in 2-3 years: CEO Salil Parekh
content: Synopsis Parekh said the business, which includes building AI agents, coding work and modernising old technology for clients, is small relative to the company's size but growing so fast that it could account for 20-30% of Infosys' work within a few quarters if the current pace continues. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Agencies Salil Parekh has wrapped up his tenure as CEO of Infosys after achieving impressive revenue growth and securing significant contracts. Infosys ' AI services, which accounted for over 8% of its revenue last quarter and are growing at a double-digit rate sequentially, are likely to drive almost half of its work in two to three years, CEO and MD Salil Parekh said on Tuesday. Parekh said the business, which includes building AI agents , coding work and modernising old technology for clients, is small relative to the company's size but growing so fast that it could account for 20-30% of Infosys' work within a few quarters if the current pace continues. "It (AI services) is growing at a fantastic pace. If you sort of extrapolate that by a few quarters, you already start to see that's 20-30% of our work in a few quarters, and maybe in two or three years, almost half of our work," Parekh said at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum 2026. He said the growth showed there was "a huge demand" for such services. Responding to questions about the viability of India's IT services industry as AI advances, Parekh said, "My own sense is it is good news for Infosys, and by sort of that same view, good news for the tech services in India". Infosys hired 20,000 college graduates last year and plans to hire another 20,000 this financial year, Parekh said. These graduates are trained in AI and then work with clients to deploy the technology and manage change. Of Infosys' 3 lakh employees, about 80,000 are already working on coding tools for clients and on some internal projects, he said. Asked how companies were adopting AI, Parekh said enterprise clients are already good users of AI services. With strong demand and capacity still being built, clients are now looking at whether they could use lower-cost tokens for the same work, considering cheaper or open-weight models instead of the most recent ones, he said. Asked whether physical infrastructure was keeping pace with AI and cloud advancements , Parekh said data had become critical to the AI ecosystem. Stricter sovereign data and cloud requirements are further restricting some of the capacity build-outs, he said. He also flagged risks in the build-out of data centres . Chips are "massively expensive" today and facing tremendous competition, and it is unclear how long the capacity being built would remain useful. New foundation models taking a different approach from the two large closed-model companies could make inference costs several times cheaper, which would also affect overall capacity, he said. "Today the demand is fantastic, but these are some of the risks that could play out," Parekh said, adding that the impact could become visible five to ten years later. He said another risk was a backlash against the build-out of AI, especially in Western markets, and that the social response needed to be balanced with the economic drivers, which "may be out of sync right now". title: High data centre, chip costs and cheaper AI models pose risks to capacity usage: Infosys CEO
content: Synopsis High data centre and chip costs, coupled with emerging AI models offering cheaper inference, pose risks to AI infrastructure investments and future capacity utilisation, Infosys CEO Salil Parekh said. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen ANI High data centre, chip costs and cheaper AI models pose risks to capacity usage: Infosys CEO High data centre and chip costs , coupled with emerging AI models offering cheaper inference, pose risks to AI infrastructure investments and future capacity utilisation, Infosys CEO Salil Parekh said. Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy 2026, the Infosys CEO highlighted that the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure comes with technological risks, particularly due to the high cost of building data centres and uncertainty over how long existing capacity will remain relevant. "In terms of the risk, I think, my sense is there is some risk in technology what we see in the cost of the buildout of the data centre capacity, the chips they are massively expensive today," he said. He further pointed out that growing competition in AI infrastructure adding, "what will be the duration of the longevity of that capacity is not clear." Parekh further noted that new foundation models are being developed using approaches different from those adopted by the two major closed-model companies, which is potentially reducing inference costs and "can affect overal capacity usage." Apart from this, he highlighted Infosys is already building AI agents for enterprise clients and developing methods to transition legacy technology to newer systems. However, he flagged, "What is critical there is really training and skilling our employees and making sure that they are available and ready to use all these techniques for our clients." Parekh said companies are increasingly examining whether they can perform the same tasks using lower-cost tokens rather than relying on the latest AI models. "...clients have started looking can we use more cost tokens for the same work...so, do we need the most recent models?," he said. Parekh further stressed, data is becoming "fastest growing commodity" particularly for large enterprises and governments. Adding data requirements are even more rigid now, he noted, rquirements of soverign cloud is further restriciting some of the capacity buildout. "We will see more and more focus on that data and how that is being scaled up for enterprise and for the sovereign nation states." Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now! title: Bumble swipes right on $1.3 billion go-private deal amid online dating industry reset
content: Synopsis Bumble said on Tuesday it had agreed to be taken private by Ithaca Holdings in a deal valued at $1.3 billion, as the dating app pushes forward with its months-long turnaround amid Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters Bumble said on Tuesday it had agreed to be taken private by Ithaca Holdings in a deal valued at $1.3 billion, as the dating app pushes forward with its months-long turnaround amid shifting Gen Z dating habits and declining paying users. Bumble and larger rival Match Group, which owns Tinder and Hinge, have been grappling with weak user engagement, particularly from younger users tired of endless swiping. Ithaca co-founders Ravi Gupta and John Hegeman will become Bumble's co-CEOs after the takeover. The private equity firm has offered $6.05 per share for Bumble, representing a 122.4% premium to the dating app's closing share price on June 24, a day before Reuters first reported the company was exploring a sale. Shares of the company soared 57% to $5.96 in premarket trading. Founded in 2014 by Whitney Wolfe Herd, Bumble pioneered the "women-first" approach to online dating. Under Herd, who returned as CEO in March 2025 after stepping down in 2023, the company has doubled down on revamping its core product with AI-powered features, group dating and a redesigned member experience in a bid to revive growth. The efforts follow steep declines in total paying users and revenue. Total paying users fell 16.4% to 3.2 million in the second quarter, while quarterly revenue has been declining for nearly two years. Bumble's market capitalization has shrunk to about $582 million as of Monday's close, a far cry from the $14 billion valuation when it went public in 2021. The company, which also owns friendship-focused Bumble For Friends, is also expanding group-based ways for people to meet, reflecting an industry-wide effort to attract Gen Z users seeking more social and less swipe-driven ways to connect. "There hasn't been a lot of innovation in the dating space for a while, and now that AI is here, the apps are going to be forced to innovate," said Liesel Sharabi, an associate professor at Arizona State University who studies online dating and relationship technology. The company entered into advanced talks to be taken private by Ithaca Holdings in a deal valuing it at roughly $1 billion, Reuters and other media outlets reported on Monday. title: Urban Company eyes Rs 2,500 crore QIP amid cash-intensive househelp battle
content: Synopsis The Gurugram-based company, which went public in September 2025, is locked in a battle with Lightspeed-backed Snabbit and General Catalyst-backed Pronto in the high cash burn instant house help industry. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen ETtech Abhiraj Singh Bhal, cofounder and CEO, Urban Company The board of home services platform Urban Company will meet on October 16 to consider a fresh fundraise, according to an exchange filing. According to sources, it is planning to raise Rs 2,000-2,500 crore via a qualified institutional placement (QIP). The Gurugram-based company, which went public in September 2025 , is locked in a battle with Lightspeed-backed Snabbit and General Catalyst-backed Pronto in the high-cash-burn instant househelp segment. Snabbit has raised a total of $112 million, including a $56-million round in April 2026. Pronto, meanwhile, has raised more than $50 million. The companies are competing in Indiaâs home services market, which was valued at $60 billion in 2024-25 and is expected to grow to $100 billion by 2029-30, according to brokerage firm Jefferies. Urban Company raised Rs 472 crore through its initial public offering (IPO) last year. As of June 30, the company had Rs 2,019 crore in cash on its books, even as its InstaHelp business continued to weigh on its bottomline. âAbout 40% of the fresh funds is expected to be allocated towards building a warchest for the InstaHelp business, while remaining is likely to be deployed towards inorganic expansion and other businesses such as India core home services, international and Native (its line of home devices),â one of the sources cited above said. Urban Company did not respond to ETâs queries. Urban Company entered the 10-minute househelp segment in early 2025, just months before its IPO, as Snabbit and Pronto were raising venture capital to compete in the space. While Urban Company initially established a lead in monthly order volumes, Bengaluru-based Snabbit caught up with its rival, while Pronto remained in third place. During the April-June quarter , Urban Companyâs InstaHelp business generated Rs 11 crore in revenues and reported adjusted operating losses of Rs 132 crore. The company said at the time that losses in the segment were expected to remain high. âAdjusted Ebitda loss per order improved from Rs 447 to Rs 346 during the quarter. Average order value declined from Rs 150 to Rs 138, reflecting continued customer acquisition through lower introductory prices as well as ongoing competitive intensity. Adjusted Ebitda loss for the quarter was Rs 132 crore. We expect losses to remain elevated as we invest to cement our leadership position. In this phase of category development, we are prioritising market leadership over everything else,â the company had said in its quarterly letter to shareholders. On a net basis, the company reported Rs 3 crore in cash burn for the April-June quarter, against Rs 75 crore in the January-March period of 2026. Urban Company, which won won the Startup of the Year award at The ET Startup Awards 2025, currently has a market capitalisation of more than Rs 25,000 crore. It had launched its IPO at a valuation of Rs 15,000 crore. As competition in the instant househelp segment plays out, Urban Companyâs core business remains profitable. The segment reported a 31% year-on-year increase in revenue to Rs 356 crore in the June quarter, while generating Rs 73 crore in adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda). title: Blume, Kalaari, Chiratae among 19 VCs in RDI fund's Rs 7,131 crore first cohort
content: Synopsis The selected cohort comprises 14 alternative investment funds (AIFs) and five focused research organisations (FROs), which will channel long-term capital into deeptech startups and private sector research and development. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Agencies Chiratae Ventures, Blume Ventures, Kalaari Capital, Speciale Invest, YourNest Capital, IvyCap Ventures, Ideaspring Capital and TVS Capital Funds are among the 19 fund managers in the first cohort of the governmentâs Rs 1 lakh crore Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) scheme. The fund has made a total commitment of Rs 7,131 crore to the cohort. The fund managers comprise 14 alternative investment funds (AIFs) and five focused research organisations (FROs), which will channel long-term capital into deeptech startups and private sector research and development. The five FROs are AI undefined Centre for Cellular and Molecular Platforms (C-CAMP) in Bengaluru; IIT Madras Research Park; Pilani Innovation undefined and Society for Innovation & Entrepreneurship (SINE) at IIT Bombay. The AIFs include Celesta India AIF Managers, AdvantEdge Investment Managers, AMA Capital Advisors, Translation Endeavors, Sixth Sense Ventures, and Campus, according to the list released by the government on Tuesday. Anusandhan National Research Foundation, the governmentâs apex research body, serves as the custodian of the â¹1 lakh crore RDI fund. The amount received by the funds is yet to be made public. Long-drawn process Sources had earlier told ET that more than 160 venture capital firms had applied to access the government-backed capital pool. The selection process focused on applicantsâ capabilities and depth of expertise in deeptech, a person familiar with the process said. The process took time as the government sought to establish a system to assess the quality and readiness of fund managers before committing public capital, an individual aware of the development said. Those not selected in the first round can address feedback received during the evaluation and apply in subsequent cohorts, they added. The government plans to announce the second cohort shortly and is open to expanding commitments depending on the quality and number of proposals received. "The distinction between commitments and drawdowns is important, as the government's commitment to a fund manager does not mean the entire amount will be released up front," the source mentioned above said. Fund managers are also expected to bring in private investment alongside government funding to help finance deeptech companies. âDisbursals will follow due process and depend on the fund managers' ability to mobilise capital and deploy it into eligible companies,â the source added. The Empowered Group of Secretaries (EGoS), at a meeting on October 8, approved the 19 organisations as second-level fund managers (SLFMs). Their applications went through a multi-stage evaluation, including an assessment of proposals and interactions with an Expert Advisory Committee, before being placed before the Executive Council of the Anusandhan National Research Foundation and the EGoS. Conflict of interest concerns The Technology Development Board (TDB), another government-designated fund manager under the RDI framework, has separately been processing proposals from companies. As of April 2026, it had received 124 proposals and approved 22 projects, with financial assistance of Rs 2,192.32 crore against a total project cost of Rs 4,743.99 crore. The TDBâs project-selection process had also faced scrutiny over potential conflicts of interest after an Indian Express investigation raised questions about investment links between some approved companies and members of the Investment Committee. The issue has brought attention to the need for transparent selection and conflict-of-interest safeguards as the government expands funding for deeptech companies. Strengthening indigenous capability Launched in November 2025, the RDI scheme aims to support high-risk, capital-intensive technology development and strengthen domestic capabilities across sectors, including artificial intelligence, robotics, space technology, quantum computing and biotechnology. The scheme follows a two-tier structure, with the government-backed fund routing capital through selected managers, which will finance eligible companies. The fund managers will channel capital to eligible enterprises undertaking research, development and innovation at Technology Readiness Level 4 and above. TRL 4 means a technologyâs components have been validated in a laboratory. This means the technology has moved beyond basic research towards validation. title: Fortnite-maker Epic Games makes 'huge pivot' with AI, CEO says
content: Synopsis Fortnite-maker Epic Games is making a "huge pivot" towards using artificial intelligence (AI) to boost video game development, CEO Tim Sweeney said on Monday. It also lands about six months after Epic said it would lay off more than 1,000 employees, though the company attributed the decision to broader issues like slower growth, rather than AI. Ramping up its use of AI internally now will increase Epic's ability "to survive the AI revolution, help other developers do the same, and come out on the other end making better code and content faster," Sweeney wrote on Monday. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Agencies Fortnite-maker Epic Games is making a "huge pivot" towards using artificial intelligence (AI) to boost video game development, CEO Tim Sweeney said on Monday. The American gaming giant is "moving developers around to retool for maximum AI acceleration," Sweeney wrote on X. "The aim isn't to do the same stuff with fewer people, but to enable everyone here to build MORE and BETTER stuff, and to bring the benefits to all teams using Unreal," he continued, referring to the company's Unreal Engine which provides game development software to third-party users. The announcement comes amid a heated debate about AI's role in art and creative sectors. It also lands about six months after Epic said it would lay off more than 1,000 employees, though the company attributed the decision to broader issues like slower growth, rather than AI. Ramping up its use of AI internally now will increase Epic's ability "to survive the AI revolution, help other developers do the same, and come out on the other end making better code and content faster," Sweeney wrote on Monday. He also pushed back on criticism from one user who replied on X that his "inability to read the room is really really astounding." "Our job, as the provider of tools and technology to much of the industry, is to design for the present that is and the future that will soon be. Personally I'm optimistic about it and see it as empowering for creators," Sweeney wrote in response. AI in game development remains controversial despite its use by the industry. More than 85 percent of game developers in Japan use AI, compared to 36 percent of developers in North America, according to PC Gamer. Epic is also reportedly delaying the release of a game developed in collaboration with Disney, according to a report from Bloomberg on Monday. The game was expected to launch in March and features characters from Marvel and Star Wars, and Epic has told employees to use an "AI first" approach to development. Epic didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now! title: Chips critical to India's future, but demand and management key to semiconductor push: N Chandrasekaran
content: Synopsis India is well placed to strengthen its role in the global semiconductor industry due to its talent base and large domestic market, but businesses must carefully assess demand and manage investments as the sector expands, Tata Sons Chairman Natarajan Chandrasekaran said. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen ANI Chips critical to India's future, but demand and management key to semiconductor push: N Chandrasekaran India is well placed to strengthen its role in the global semiconductor industry due to its talent base and large domestic market, but businesses must carefully assess demand and manage investments as the sector expands, Tata Sons Chairman Natarajan Chandrasekaran said. Speaking during a panel discussion titled 'The End of Predictability' at Bloomberg New Economy 2026, Chandrasekaran said, "Chips are the future. Chips are going to be fundamentally required for domestic institution," highlighting the growing importance of semiconductors for India's industrial and technological development. He said India had the potential to contribute to the global semiconductor industry, supported by its workforce and domestic demand. However, he cautioned that companies would need to remain mindful of market requirements and management as they make investment decisions. "We have to be also be careful because you need to keep an eye on management. We need to also see where the demand is," he said, stressing that investment decisions should account for the needs of businesses, people and the country's future. Chandrasekaran's comments come as Tata Group advances its semiconductor manufacturing plans in India. Tata Electronics is establishing a semiconductor fabrication facility in Dholera, Gujarat, with support from Dutch technology company ASML under an agreement signed in May. The partnership is intended to support the facility's establishment and expansion. Separately, Tata's semiconductor assembly and testing facility in Jagiroad, Assam, is expected to produce up to 48 million chips per day. The facility is expected to serve sectors including automobiles, telecommunications, consumer electronics and AI-driven devices. The projects form part of Tata's efforts to build semiconductor manufacturing capabilities in India, spanning chip fabrication as well as assembly and testing. At the panel discussion, Chandrasekaran had also highlighted the broader effects of technological change, including the potential misuse of advanced technologies and the need to restructure labour markets in the near term. He said technology could deliver significant benefits over the medium to long term, while warning that ongoing conflicts remained a concern. His latest remarks underline the importance of matching India's semiconductor ambitions with viable demand and effective management as companies develop manufacturing capacity and seek a role in global supply chains. title: US reverses course on Britain's testing of AI models
content: Synopsis American AI developers can give the British government early access to AI models for safety testing without running afoul of US President Donald Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters Letters spelling "AI," a keyboard and a robotic hand in this illustration created on September 23, 2026. American AI developers can give the British government early access to AI models for safety testing without running afoul of US President Donald Trump's administration, the Telegraph newspaper said on Sunday. The Trump administration has reversed a decision that requested developers such as OpenAI and Anthropic not to share new AI models with Britain's AI Security Institute before release, the newspaper said. The change signals a softer stance by the Trump administration on international AI safety efforts, giving US developers greater latitude to cooperate with Britain as policymakers grapple with how to oversee the increasingly powerful technology. Spokespersons for Trump, OpenAI and Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Reuters. Britain's AI Security Institute, set up after the world's first AI safety summit in 2023, tests the most advanced AI models to evaluate their capabilities and the risk of misuse. Trump has repeatedly dismissed calls for binding safety requirements on AI developers, a position that appears to be shifting. His newly launched AI task force said on Friday developers must report security incidents with their AI models. Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now! title: TSMC expected to report sixth straight quarter of record profit thanks to AI boom
content: Synopsis Analysts say demand for Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co's (TSMC) AI chipmaking capacity, as well as its advanced chip packaging technology, CoWoS, remains strong. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters FILE PHOTO: The logo of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) at the company's second-quarter earnings conference in Taipei, Taiwan, July 16, 2026. TSMC , the world's largest manufacturer of advanced AI chips , will likely report a sixth consecutive quarter of record earnings, driven by booming infrastructure spending in the tech sector. Analysts say demand for Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co's (TSMC) AI chipmaking capacity, as well as its advanced chip packaging technology, CoWoS, remains strong. That has catapulted Asia's most valuable company, a key supplier to Nvidia and Apple, to new heights. Its market capitalisation is almost double that of South Korean rival Samsung Electronics at around $2.1 trillion. On Thursday, TSMC is expected to report a 65% surge in third-quarter net profit to T$746.3 billion ($23.4 billion), according to an LSEG SmartEstimate compiled from 16 analysts. SmartEstimates place greater weight on forecasts from analysts who are more consistently accurate. An earnings call at which it will provide fourth-quarter and updated full-year guidance is scheduled for 0600 GMT. Any result above T$706.56 billion would mark the company's highest-ever quarterly net income, as well as its 11th consecutive quarter of profit growth. Last Thursday, it posted a 50% year-on-year rise in third-quarter revenue, beating market forecasts and hitting a new record high. In an October 6 report, Morgan Stanley analyst Charlie Chan said he expected TSMC to raise its full-year revenue growth forecast to the low-to-mid 40% range from its current guidance of more than 40%, driven by strong demand for its 3-nanometre chips. TEXAS EXPANSION PROSPECTS TSMC is investing $265 billion to build chip factories in the US state of Arizona, including an additional $100 billion that was unveiled in July. In September, Reuters reported that TSMC was evaluating a potential investment in Texas. Tesla CEO Elon Musk also said last week that his companies would build and operate the Terafab AI chip complex, with TSMC potentially subleasing a part of it. Analysts expect TSMC to address questions about its potential expansion plans in Texas. In his report, Chan said an expansion in Texas could become necessary given growing customer demand and limited space at TSMC's Arizona site in five years' time. Phelix Lee, senior equity analyst at Morningstar, however, saw limited urgency for TSMC to expand into Texas, given that some of its planned fabs in Arizona have yet to be built. "Texas is a good location for a 2030s or 2040s expansion grand plan, given its long history of semiconductor ecosystem and talent pool," Lee said. "It may be a dangling carrot to preempt potential US trade and other policies." On its July earnings call, the company raised its capex forecast for this year to between $60 billion and $64 billion from a previous prediction at the high end of $52 billion to $56 billion. TSMC's Taipei-listed shares have gained 63% so far this year, broadly in line with a 69% rise for the broader market. Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!
