title: ETSA champions show the great Indian dream is all home-brewed and visa-free: Union Minister Piyush Goyal
content: Synopsis In a candid conversation with ETâs Deepshikha Sikarwar, he spoke about Indiaâs trade deals, India-US relations, foreign investment, and how Indian businesses will benefit from the restrictions on the green card programme. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen ETtech Commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal was the guest of honour at the ETSA event , days after returning from the US where he attended the G20 Trade Ministersâ Meeting and held discussions on a trade agreement with the Trump administration. In a candid conversation with ETâs Deepshikha Sikarwar, he spoke about Indiaâs trade deals, India-US relations, foreign investment, and how Indian businesses will benefit from the restrictions on the green card programme . Edited excerpts: Where is the India-US relationship headed, with various statements that have come in the past two days? Two countries where the leaders, governments, businesses and the people are quite intrinsically engaged with each other will always have certain friction points. But at the same time, there is recognition in both countries that this is a relationship which is very consequential. It is a relationship that both countries would like to nurture for the future. I would not read too much into every single incident or every single comment. My own submission to you would be to look at the longer-term impact that this relationship will have on the global economy, and youâll realise that we are friends, and we will continue to be very good friends. The IT and tech sectors have concerns over the decisions on H-1B visas and the green card programmeâ¦ Not at all. In fact, I heard Tata (Consultancy Services) say that they will not be hit at all by this. I personally have never ever raised the issue of H-1B visas or green cards in my conversations with the US, particularly in the last seven and a half years as commerce minister. Immigration is not an FTA issue, nor is it directly related to trade. What relates to trade is mobility, and mobility to provide a service is very essential. Every country has the right to monitor and regulate. We would not like people from across the world to have open access to our country. I personally believe that not getting more H-1B visas is absolutely good for the Indian economy. Some of our best talent over the last, particularly 25-30 years has gone away to the US, and I see the billionaires of Indian origin literally down every street. I wonder what would have happened if all of them had been doing their businesses in India. After the Covid pandemic, things have changed dramatically. You donât need to be physically present to do a lot of the things. It is only a few people who may need to go and certainly there should not be a problem for those people. The larger bulk of the work is now coming to Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Gurugram, Noida, Mumbai. Businesses are understanding the value of having their global capability centres in India. Not getting H-1B visas is going to create probably a greater thrust to the startup ecosystem. Weâve only just begun. In the deep tech space, we can still count the startups of significance in a few thousands. We have a long way to go. Every one of these spaces â defence, or research institutions â the educational institutions of eminence across the world, has significant Indian presence at the leadership and operating levels. You can get better, if not the best, in that profession in India, at maybe one-fifth or one-sixth that value. He will be paying taxes in India, sitting in infrastructure created in India and living with his family, which is not necessarily a luxury all these H-1B persons get when they go to the US. He will be spending in India and consuming the goods and services that all our entrepreneurs, businesses, and startups will provide. So, look at the entire ecosystem, and you will realise every H-1B visa not granted is a big win for India. Are some US companies looking at scaling up operations here? Not some, all of them, because this is where the talent is. Where are we on the bilateral trade deal? US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the deal is not imminent, and the government here has said talks have plateaued. We are talking to each other because circumstances have significantly changed from the first week of February when we shook hands and announced the deal. The (US) Supreme Court took away the powers of the President to have the IEEPA (International Emergency Economic Powers Act) tariffs. Since then, they have been working on different models to bring in tariffs and to give competitive advantage to those who do deals with them. A free trade agreement is basically giving your trading partner access to your market at a preferential rate or in a preferential manner compared to the competition. So, I donât have to necessarily always make everything at zero duty. The Modi government has only focused on developed, rich and prosperous countries. With our nine FTAs, we cover 38 developed countries, all of them having per capita income significantly more than India, economies significantly more prosperous than India, where we donât directly compete. We actually complement each other. Products that we want to sell, they just cannot make at this price. The products that they want to offer, we need them in India. We need GPUs, data centre equipment and best of class defence equipment from America. India would have preferential access to $85 trillion of GDP with all its trade agreements. Thatâs what we are trying to unlock for all our startups, entrepreneurs and businesses. Now, obviously, thereâs a lot of hard bargaining. So, when the honourable finance minister says things have plateaued, from all that she said, you picked up only the headline. We have the UK FTA in the bag, EU almost doneâ¦ Itâs totally done. The India FTA will be the fastest approval process that the EU has ever done. On January 27, we announced closure and by early next year, it will come into force. In our FTA with 27 nations on the other side (EU), not one nation is opposing an item. Thereâs 100% unanimity in the EU. Our negotiations with the US are on a steady keel. When you look at the text of what the honourable FM said, she said weâve concluded the deal. We have nothing more to give or to take. And the fine print is being worked upon. The basic element is how they will give us the comparative advantage, which we had agreed upon in February, and that requires a little bit of legal acumen, which AI cannot give, because this is going beyond the textbook, and thatâs what we are working on. Did you get some assurance from the US on the proposed punitive tariffs on Russian oil? The world recognises the quality of oil that Indian refineries use, the sour medium quality of oil largely comes from the Middle East or from Russia. There are some refineries which can use the quality of oil that the US makes. They are buying a lot of oil from the US. A lot of our gas comes from the US. Our ideal case scenario is to have a very diversified portfolio of countries. We would like Canada to also supply our energy needs. We are a self-respecting country. We have to protect our national interests. Weâve seen outflows in the capital markets and FDI as well. Why is FDI not being sticky? The levels we have reached in our artificial intelligence story are still not significant enough for the stock market or listing of our AI companies. The story that we have seen of stock market outflows largely is because of the greater attraction of technology stocks in the West or other developed countries. Now, with interest rate differential between US bonds and Indian bonds also being significantly lessâ¦itâs quite natural that we will see some slowing down of flows. Whatâs next for domestic startups ? We are willing to fund whatever it takes to take our startups to the rest of the world. Please identify every single exhibition, conference, seminar, or opportunity to showcase our startups. Bharat Innovates, which we took to Nice (France)â¦130 of our best startups in the deeptech space, selected out of 3,000. So, if we can take our Indian startups to the world, the government, my ministry, is ready to support. We need to think big. Letâs get out of the cosy comfort of the large Indian opportunity or Indian market. Letâs think of going global, because those who will not, will be left behind. We have to offer this to the world, and not be dependent on their intelligence coming to India. Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now! title: ETSA 2026: A secret circle, cosmic sparks and the night tech elite got goosebumps
content: Synopsis The Closed-door Manifesto The unscripted room where minister Goyalâs call to arms met Bengaluruâs spirit, inspiring a tech elite primed for global dominance. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen ETtech An intimate and candid closed-door interaction with commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal was a surprise even to the winners of the 12th Economic Times Startup Awards . Then again, ETSA is where unexpected delight happens by design. It started as an impromptu circle around the minister just after the ceremony. Someone proposed shifting to the winnersâ room next door, and soon everyone was huddled around the table. There the crÃ¨me de la crÃ¨me of Indiaâs startups sat in rapt attention, taking in every word from a visibly buoyed minister. The conversation ranged from trade shenanigans in the US to the importance of yoga, and from Indiaâs private sector firing rockets successfully at first attempt to why it is imperative to pump more capital into the startup ecosystem. The minister underlined the need for more open conversations to bridge the spirit of Bengaluru and the intent of Delhi. âYou tell us what you need,â he emphasised. To nurture and nourish the next wave, he challenged the founders to pay it forward by reinvesting profits into emerging startups, while urging family offices to put their heft and capital behind domestic entrepreneurs. The startup crowd in the room was over the moon with the impromptu interaction. Pallavi Mohadikar, cofounder and CEO of Palmonas, one of this yearâs ETSA winners, said that the interaction felt like a breath of fresh air. She shared her key takeaway from the interaction. âThings are simple; you donât need to complicate them. You just need to sort them out in your head,â she said. âWhen Piyush Goyal was speaking about taking India to the world, it felt like somebody understood what weâre trying to do. Weâre trying to build a global brand from India. It was one of those moments when you get goosebumps and feel youâre on the right track.â This was also the evening when the chatter went high on deeptech. The ETSA journey, in its 12th edition, is also reflective of the gradual shift in Indiaâs startup focus, from consumer tech to space, semiconductor, robotics and AI. Even so, Paras Chopra, cofounder of Wingify, made a key point about the paucity of AI startups : âThatâs the biggest missing piece I feel.â Progress on that, he added, should come from the entrepreneurs. title: ET Startup Awards 2026 | Govt backing and patient capital propel India's leap into AI and chips: Satyan Gajwani
content: Synopsis Gajwani said the ecosystem, once driven by fintech, food delivery, SaaS, commerce, quick commerce and direct-to-consumer brands, was witnessing founders focused on deep, proprietary technology. Indian startups are now building semiconductor chips, AI, robotics, clean energy technologies and new materials, while investors are shaping funds, willing to wait longer for these companies to mature. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen ETtech Satyan Gajwani, chairman, Times Internet Indiaâs startup ecosystem is maturing and entering a new era of deep technology , said Satyan Gajwani, chairman of Times Internet, in his address at the ET Startup Awards 2026 , citing the launch of launch vehicle Vikram-1 as a milestone in the countryâs technological ambitions. On July 18, the rocket, built by Hyderabad-based startup, Skyroot Aerospace , lifted off from Sriharikota and placed customer satellites in orbit 450 kilometres above earth. âWith that launch, India became only the third nation after the US and China with a private company able to reach space,â Gajwani said. ETSA 2026 jury member Mukesh Bansal was Skyroot's first investor. Gajwani said the ecosystem, once driven by fintech, food delivery, SaaS, commerce, quick commerce and direct-to-consumer brands, was witnessing founders focused on deep, proprietary technology. Indian startups are now building semiconductor chips , AI, robotics, clean energy technologies and new materials, while investors are shaping funds, willing to wait longer for these companies to mature. âThis maturing of the Indian startup ecosystem, this energy, and this audacity, founders paying it forward as investors, the structural backing by the state, they've all come together thanks to a lot of advocacy and championing by many of our leaders. And foremost among them has been Piyush Goyal, minister of Commerce and Industry,â said Gajwani. He credited government support, regulatory reforms and entrepreneurial leadership for accelerating this transition. Under Startup India , the number of recognised startups has grown from a few hundred to more than 250,000, creating nearly 2.5 million jobs. A Rs 10,000 crore Fund of Funds has also been launched to support new-age sectors. Gajwani also highlighted startupsâ role in formalising informal work and building new Indian brands. However, he cautioned that India remains behind the US and China in artificial intelligence. âClosing that gap will take deep research, serious compute, entrepreneurial vision and patient capital,â he said. âBut if a startup can put a rocket into orbit from Sriharikota, I have no doubt this ecosystem can build AI that the world will want to use,â Gajwani added. Striking a balance between boardroom polish and founder-casual ease, guests rounded off their looks with smart rings and trackers, turning the eveningâs uniform into something more personal and data-driven. title: ET Startup Awards 2026 | Tier-II cities rechart startup geography: IDFC First Bank’s Vaidyanathan
content: Synopsis The startup story is not confined to a handful of sectors or cities, but is being shaped by talent and ideas across the country, Vaidyanathan said. About 52% of the startups banking with IDFC First Bank come from tier-II and -III locations, reflecting the widening geography of entrepreneurship, he said. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen ETtech Phenomenal companies are being created in India and the startup ecosystem is expanding beyond the familiar technology hubs, said V Vaidyanathan, chief executive and managing director of IDFC First Bank . âThe range of applications we are seeing today, including satellite technology, hyperspectral imaging, AI-enabled brain mapping and advances in computing, demonstrate the ambition and technical talent driving Indiaâs startup ecosystem,â Vaidyanathan said at the ET Startup Awards event. The startup story is not confined to a handful of sectors or cities, but is being shaped by talent and ideas across the country, Vaidyanathan said. About 52% of the startups banking with IDFC First Bank come from tier-II and -III locations, reflecting the widening geography of entrepreneurship, he said. The growth of the ecosystem depends on practical support that helps young companies move from an idea to a functioning business, and access to finance, suitable banking services and advice on managing funds can be as important to a startupâs progress as its technology and ability to attract investment, he said. Vaidyanathan advised founders to pay greater attention to how they manage their money. Startups often raise capital from investors but may leave funds in accounts that do not earn interest; entrepreneurs should understand their options and make their cash work more effectively, he said. title: ETSA 2026: Over a decade on, India's startup story is only getting started
content: Synopsis The 12th edition of The Economic Times Startup Awards (ETSA) captured this transition, reflecting an ecosystem that has moved beyond the race for scale to pursue technological depth, durable businesses and international markets. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen ETtech Winners of ET Startup Awards 2026 with Union minister Piyush Goyal and Times Internet chairman Satyan Gajwani More than a decade after Indiaâs startup ecosystem took its first steps, its entrepreneurial journey is entering a new phase, with a growing crop of founders tackling complex problems in deeptech and hardtech, and homegrown companies tapping the public markets as well as pursuing global ambitions. The 12th edition of The Economic Times Startup Awards (ETSA) captured this transition, reflecting an ecosystem that has moved beyond the race for scale to pursue technological depth, durable businesses and international markets. That breadth was evident in this yearâs Startup of the Year nominees, which included AI startup Sarvam, ecommerce marketplace Meesho , satellite launch vehicle maker Skyroot, wealthtech platform Groww , urban mobility service Rapido and logistics company Porter. An 11-member jury , chaired by Wipro executive chairman Rishad Premji, named Groww the winner , recognising its ability to sustain rapid growth while turning profitable at scale. Speaking to a gathering of more than 300 of the most influential names in Indiaâs startup and technology industry, commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal, the guest of honour at the awards, pointed to the gap between the scale of the countryâs startup ecosystem and its untapped potential. Even with about 250,000 registered startups, he said, the journey was only beginning, particularly in deeptech, where the number of significant startups remains small. âWe have only just begun,â said the minister. âIn fact, in the deeptech space, there are only a few thousand startups of significance. We have a long way to go.â Also Read: ETSA champions show the great Indian dream is all home-brewed and visa-free His remarks reflect a broader shift in an ecosystem, where the aspiration is increasingly to build companies that can compete internationally, rather than simply serve Indiaâs growing consumer base. The early years of the startup boom were dominated by ecommerce, consumer internet and digital services, but founders are taking on problems in sectors that demand deeper technological capabilities, longer investment horizons and greater spending on research and development. Many prominent voices from the industry concurred. Kalyan Krishnamurthy, chief executive of Flipkart group, termed Indiaâs startup ecosystem one of the most dynamic stories of this time. âIt keeps growing in ambition, in scale and in the problems it takes on,â he said. âFounders, investors, operators and customers are all building on each other's progress. ETSA does an important job in celebrating that journey and the entrepreneurs driving it.â PhonePe cofounder and chief executive Sameer Nigam said Indiaâs startup landscape had widened dramatically over the past decade, with innovation spreading well beyond its early strongholds. âWe started with companies largely focused on consumer technology and ecommerce,â he said. âToday, we are seeing startups working in deeptech, agritech, robotics and foundational technologies. The ET Startup Awards reflect that innovation taking place across the country.â Razorpay cofounder and CEO Harshil Mathur, whose company was Startup of the Year at ETSA 2022 , said the strength of this yearâs field showed how far Indian entrepreneurship had come. âEach of them was outstanding, and choosing a winner must have been extremely difficult. It shows how far the ecosystem has come. Ultimately, the ecosystem wins when more companies do well,â he said. Manu Chandra, founder and managing partner at venture capital firm Sauce, won the Midas Touch award for distinguished early-stage consumer investing. Online yoga platform Habuild was named Bootstrap Champ , while climatetech startup Varaha won the Social Enterprise award . For the first time, the Woman Ahead category had joint winners , with the jury picking Palmonas cofounder and CEO Pallavi Mohadikar and Progcap cofounder and chief executive Pallavi Shrivastava. Deeptech startup Theranautilus won the Top Innovator award , Armatrix was named Best on Campus startup , and Mukund Jha, cofounder of vibe-coding startup Emergent, was the Comeback Kid . The next chapter Discussions in Bengaluru on Friday also made it clear that global ambition will define the ecosystemâs next phase. âLetâs get out of the cosy comfort of the large Indian opportunity or Indian market. Let us think of going global, because those who will not go global will be left behind,â Goyal said. Indiaâs lower cost structure is an advantage, but it cannot make up for inferior technology, Dheemanth Nagaraj, cofounder and CEO of AI semiconductor startup Agrani Labs, said during a panel discussion on building the hard stuff . Moderated by Accel founding partner Prashanth Prakash, the panel also included Kshitij Khandelwal, cofounder and CTO of spacetech startup Pixxel, and Laina Emmanuel, cofounder and chief executive of BrainSight AI. âAt the end of the day, the technology we use is state of the art. Thereâs no other way to penetrate the market,â Nagaraj said, arguing that a cheaper but substandard product would not work. For the ecosystemâs next phase of growth, however, access to capital and viable exit routes will be critical. In a fireside chat, Groww cofounder and CEO Lalit Keshre said capital was available for companies that needed it, but valuations remained a key consideration for private market investors. Also Read: List when the business is predictable, and stay transparent after: Groww, Meesho founders Meesho cofounder and chief executive Vidit Aatrey said global late-stage investors, many of whom have been focused on AI in recent years, would return to India as they reassess opportunities across markets. âLate-stage funds have been comparing opportunities across the globeâ¦ and we all know the last two to three years have been about AI. I believe they will come back to India and it will happen very soon,â he said. Serial entrepreneur K Ganesh said three developments were reinforcing one another â investors were more willing to back founders for longer, public markets were accepting new-age companies that continued to invest for growth, and entrepreneurs were taking on harder problems in sectors such as semiconductors, space, defence and energy. âEvery successful IPO gives investors a reason to fund the next deeptech company,â Ganesh said. The Economic Times Startup Awards were presented by IDFC First Bank, with workspace partner Indiqube, knowledge partner Tracxn and hospitality partner The Leela Palace, Bengaluru. Global investor Qualcomm Ventures divested nearly a 1% stake in logistics solutions provider Shadowfax Technologies for Rs 157 crore through an open market transaction on Monday. Qualcomm Ventures, through its affiliate Qualcomm Asia Pacific Pte Ltd, sold a little over 57.13 lakh shares, representing a 0.98% stake, in Bengaluru-based Shadowfax Technologies , according to bulk deal data on the BSE. title: Govt selects 19 fund managers under RDI, committing Rs 7,131 crore
content: Synopsis The government's Research, Development and Innovation Fund (RDIF) has approved its first cohort of 19 second-level fund managers with a total commitment of Rs 7,131 crore, marking a key step towards mobilising private investment in research and development and emerging technologies. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Agencies The government has selected 19 fund managers for its Rs 1 lakh crore Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) scheme, committing Rs 7,131 crore to the first cohort as it looks to channel long-term capital into deeptech startups and private sector research and development. Sources told ET that more than 160 venture capital firms had applied to access the government-backed capital pool. Out of the 19 selected 14 are Alternative Investment Fund (AIFs) and five are Focused Research Organisations (FROs). As reported by ET earlier, applicants included Mela Ventures, Blume Ventures, Ideaspring Capital, 3one4 Capital, Chiratae Ventures, Wyser Capital, Waterbridge Ventures, Ankur Capital and pi Ventures, among others. The government is yet to release the list of the 19 fund managers. The selection process focused on the applicants' capabilities and depth of expertise in deeptech, a person familiar with the process told ET on condition of anonymity. "The process took time as the government sought to put in place a robust system to assess the quality and readiness of fund managers before committing public capital," they added. The government also plans to announce the second cohort shortly, sources said. "Applicants who were not selected in the first round can address the feedback received during the evaluation and reapply in subsequent cohorts," the person said. Not being selected in the first round does not rule out their participation in later rounds. The government is also open to expanding commitments depending on the quality and number of proposals received. While the scheme has an overall corpus of Rs 1 lakh crore, the actual drawdown will depend on the progress of selected fund managers, their ability to raise matching capital from private investors and the pace at which funding can be deployed into eligible companies. The Empowered Group of Secretaries (EGoS), at a meeting held on October 8, approved 14 alternative investment funds (AIFs) and five focused research organisations (FROs) as second-level fund managers (SLFMs), the Department of Science and Technology said in a statement on Monday. The first call for applications from prospective fund managers was launched in January 2026. The applications went through a multi-stage evaluation process, including an assessment of proposals and in-person interactions with an Expert Advisory Committee. The proposals were subsequently placed before the Executive Council of the Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF) and the EGoS for approval. "The distinction between commitments and drawdowns is important, as the government's commitment to a fund manager does not mean the entire amount will be released upfront. Disbursements will follow due process and depend on the fund managers' ability to mobilise capital and deploy it into eligible companies," the source mentioned above said. The Technology Development Board (TDB), one of the governmentâs second-level fund managers under the RDI scheme, has already begun deploying capital. TDB had received 124 proposals by April 2026, of which it had approved 22 projects, with financial assistance of Rs 2,192 crore against a total project cost of Rs 4,744 crore. Companies including Dhruva Space, Agnikul Cosmos, The ePlane Company, Ather Energy , GalaxEye and Noccarc Robotics, across sectors such as space technology, electric mobility, robotics and healthcare have received the approval. The selected fund managers will use the capital to fund technology enterprises undertaking research, development and innovation at Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 4 and above. The scheme is designed to support technologies that have progressed beyond the early research stage but require further development and financing before commercial deployment. Launched in November 2025, the RDI scheme aims to address the financing gap for high-risk, capital-intensive technology development and encourage private sector investment in strategic and emerging technology areas. The scheme follows a two-tier structure, with the government-backed Special Purpose Fund housed within ANRF channelling capital through selected second-level fund managers, which then finance eligible companies. The scheme is expected to support research and development across areas such as artificial intelligence, quantum computing, robotics, space technology and biotechnology, with the broader objective of strengthening domestic technology capabilities and reducing dependence on imported technologies. title: Microsoft plans huge deployment of its own AI chips, with an eye on saving costs
content: Synopsis The Maia 300, as the chip is called, is the third generation of the company's custom chips designed to handle AI data crunching such as coding and carrying out complex business tasks on a user's behalf. Its predecessor is already running Microsoft's in-house AI models, as well as models from OpenAI delivered on Microsoft's Azure cloud computing service. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters Microsoft CEO Satya Madella speaks at Microsoft Windows & Surface event where new on-device AI capabilities for Windows PCs using Nvidia's new RTX Spark chips were announced, in San Francisco, Microsoft announced the next generation of its custom AI chip on Monday and said it plans to deploy potentially more than a million of them next year to back its internal AI services. The Maia 300 , as the chip is called, is the third generation of the company's custom chips designed to handle AI data crunching such as coding and carrying out complex business tasks on a user's behalf. Its predecessor is already running Microsoft's in-house AI models, as well as models from OpenAI delivered on Microsoft's Azure cloud computing service. The new version comes amid a flurry of custom chips from both cloud computing rivals and AI firms such as OpenAI aimed at loosening the hold of Nvidia on the AI computing market . To construct the chip, Microsoft took a different technical path from Nvidia whose AI accelerators use one massive computing chip surrounded by high-bandwidth memory chips. The central computing processor in Microsoft's Maia 300 silicon is composed of "chiplets" - typically specialized chips bonded together - that use 2-nanometer technology from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co for key computing functions. Other chiplets included in the design use cheaper 3-nanometer tech for functions such as moving data off the processor and elsewhere inside the system. The Maia 300 processors will go into racks that contain 96 chips and use about 167 kilowatts of power, compared with the 142 kilowatts used by Nvidia's most recent GB300 AI server racks with 72 of its graphics processing units (GPUs). Microsoft said the Maia 300 chips will get about 40% more useful computing done per megawatt than "leading GPU-based systems," though it did not name the systems it used for a comparison. "It's basically delivering more intelligence for every watt, every dollar, and every byte of memory by optimizing across the entire system," Rani Borkar, president of Azure hardware systems and infrastructure at Microsoft, told Reuters in an interview. Microsoft said it plans to roll out "multi-gigawatt deployments" of the Maia 300 chip starting next year. Microsoft has said it expects to spend more than $175 billion in capital expenditures this calendar year. Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now! title: The Wealth Company AIF invests Rs 400 crore in Boldfit
content: Synopsis Founded in 2018 by Pallav Bihani, Boldfit offers sportswear, athletic footwear, sports equipment, and fitness essentials. It has grown at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of more than 80% over the past three years and serves over 2 crore customers annually, according to a company statement. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen ETtech The Wealth Company Alternates, part of the Pantomath Group , has invested around Rs 400 crore in fitness and sports products brand Boldfit as part of its series B funding , the company announced on Monday. The investment will support Boldfitâs expansion into physical retail, product innovation, and manufacturing, as well as acquisitions to strengthen its presence across categories. Founded in 2018 by Pallav Bihani, Boldfit offers sportswear, athletic footwear, sports equipment, and fitness essentials. It has grown at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of more than 80% over the past three years and serves over 2 crore customers annually, according to a company statement. Boldfit had previously raised Rs 110 crore from Bessemer Venture Partners in its series A round in 2024. Sportspersons KL Rahul and Sania Mirza are among its investors. The investment marks the fourth major deal by the Bharat Value Fund in the past 12 months, following investments in Zetwerk Manufacturing, Amnex Infotechnologies, and Big Mishra. The fund has deployed an average of around Rs 400 crore across these investments. Indiaâs fitness and sports goods market is estimated at approximately $16 billion and projected to grow at a CAGR of 16%, reaching $35 by FY31, underpinned by rising disposable income, a young population, growing health awareness, and adoption of an active lifestyle and athleisure. âIndia is undergoing a fundamental shift in how it engages with fitness and sports. Active living is no longer confined to a facility or occasional play â it is transitioning into a frequent household habit across the country,â said Madhu Lunawat, founder and whole-time director, Wealth Company Asset Management Private Limited. âOur ambition is to see India become a sporting powerhouse, with greater participation, stronger sporting talent, and many more medals on the world stage. Boldfit intends to play a meaningful role in that transformation,â said Bihani, whoâs also the CEO of Boldfit. title: IonQ to buy cybersecurity firm Elisity in up to $1.3 billion deal
content: Synopsis Quantum computing company IonQ said on Monday it would buy cybersecurity firm Elisity in an all-stock deal valued at up to $1.3 billion, as it looks to expand its quantum security business. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters Quantum computing company IonQ said on Monday it would buy cybersecurity firm Elisity in an all-stock deal valued at up to $1.3 billion, as it looks to expand its quantum security business. IonQ said the acquisition would provide it with expanded channels to bring its quantum offerings to both enterprise and government customers , helping them deal with current threats and prepare for attacks from future quantum computers. Elisity, founded in 2019, has more than 100 customer deployments worldwide and has doubled its revenue and customer base year-over-year, IonQ said. The deal value includes up to $150 million in earn-outs tied to Elisity's performance, it added. The number of IonQ shares to be issued will be calculated at a price between $33.07 and $49.61 per share. " Q-Day is coming much faster than predicted," IonQ CEO Niccolo de Masi said, referring to the point when quantum computers could break widely used encryption. Elisity CEO James Winebrenner will continue to lead the acquired business after the deal closes. The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, subject to regulatory approval. IonQ completed its acquisition of chipmaker SkyWater Technology earlier this year to bring semiconductor manufacturing in-house and boost the development of its next-generation quantum processors. title: Norway fines Microsoft's Xandr $9.6 million over Grindr data sharing
content: Synopsis Xandr relayed data revealing the sexual orientation of users of Grindr, a dating app for LGBTQIA+ people, to companies in automated ad auctions from July 2018 to April 2020. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters Grindr app is seen on a mobile phone in this photo illustration taken in Shanghai, China March 28, 2019. Norway's data protection authority has fined Microsoft's adtech unit Xandr 92 million crowns ($9.61 million) for unlawfully relaying Grindr users' sensitive data to thousands of advertisers, it said on Monday. Xandr relayed data revealing the sexual orientation of users of Grindr, a dating app for LGBTQIA+ people, to companies in automated ad auctions from July 2018 to April 2020. It is the biggest fine the Norwegian authority has issued, and targets the advertising middlemen rather than the app itself. The regulator said companies that traded in people's data could not pass the blame to others. The data protection authority fined Grindr 65 million crowns over the same breaches in 2021. The fine was based on Xandr's revenue, not Microsoft's, which did not own the unit at the time. Xandr has three weeks to appeal. Xandr said it assumed Grindr had obtained users' consent and never checked, the data protection authority said. It rejected that argument and ruled Xandr shared legal responsibility with Grindr. Microsoft said the privacy of users was a top priority. "This investigation and decision focused on conduct that predates Microsoft's acquisition of Xandr, and in that time the interpretation and application of legal standards and practices has continued to evolve. We are reviewing the decision and assessing our options," it said. The case began with a 2020 complaint by the Norwegian Consumer Council, whose research exposed how apps shared user data, and Austrian data privacy organisation noyb, which called the decision "a valuable precedent". title: Philippine lower house approves bill restricting minors' social media access
content: Synopsis The Philippines is the latest country, from Greece and Portugal to Australia, Malaysia and Indonesia, to try to curb social media use by minors, as concern grows over its effects on child health and safety. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters The Philippines on Monday moved a step closer to restricting social media use among minors after its lower house of Congress approved a measure banning access to platforms for children under 13. The Philippines is the latest country, from Greece and Portugal to Australia, Malaysia and Indonesia, to try to curb social media use by minors, as concern grows over its effects on child health and safety. The House of Representatives voted overwhelmingly in favour of limiting minors' access to social media platforms, following on from the Senate's recent endorsement of a similar bill. The two chambers will now be required to reconcile their bills then submit a final draft for presidential approval. The progress of the legislation comes after three school shootings since June in the Philippines that reignited debate over children accessing social media and online content. A 16-year-old last month shot dead at least two fellow students before turning the gun on himself, while in August, a â student live-streamed himself shooting and killing a classmate before taking his own life. Gun violence at schools was previously rare in the Philippines. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr said on Sunday he had been studying the bill passed by the Senate and that a blanket ban on social media could cause children to hide their online activities, leaving them vulnerable to grooming and abuse. The Senate's version is stricter than the draft approved by the lower house and bans anyone under 18 from creating social media accounts. TikTok, YouTube owner Alphabet, and Meta Platforms , the owner of Facebook and Instagram, did not immediately respond to separate requests for comment on the Philippines house passing the bill. Neighbouring Malaysia in June began barring under-16s from registering accounts on social media platforms, which are required to conduct age verification against government-issued records. Malaysia has given social platforms until January 2027 to implement the measure. Indonesia issued a regulation in March requiring social media firms with platforms it deems high risk to deactivate accounts belonging to children under 16, which have so far included X, Instagram and video game platform Roblox. As of last week, TikTok has deactivated around 9 million accounts belonging to children under 16 in Indonesia, while Meta has blocked 85,000 Instagram accounts and 99,000 Facebook accounts. title: GE Aerospace to nearly double supplier spend in India by 2030, eyes growing aviation demand
content: Synopsis The announcement was made alongside the release of a report by Ernst & Young (EY), titled 'Powering Progress: GE Aerospace's Economic Impact in India', which assesses the company's economic contribution to India's commercial aviation, defence, manufacturing and engineering sectors over four decades. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen ANI GE Aerospace to nearly double supplier spend in India by 2030, eyes growing Aviation demand GE Aerospace has announced plans to nearly double its spending on Indian suppliers between 2025 and 2030, as the company looks to strengthen its domestic supply chain and support India's rapidly expanding aviation sector. The announcement was made alongside the release of a report by Ernst & Young (EY), titled 'Powering Progress: GE Aerospace's Economic Impact in India', which assesses the company's economic contribution to India's commercial aviation, defence, manufacturing and engineering sectors over four decades. The report was released at India Taking Flight - Aviation, Innovation and the Road to Viksit Bharat 2047, an event hosted by GE Aerospace and attended by industry leaders. According to the report, GE Aerospace spent approximately $200 million on its Indian supply chain in 2025. The company plans to double this expenditure by 2030 to meet rising demand and expand its network of domestic suppliers, including small and medium-sized enterprises. India's commercial aviation sector continues to witness significant growth, with domestic airlines generating approximately $19 billion in revenue in the financial year 2025-26 (FY26). GE Aerospace's advanced engine technology and operational reliability contribute to the efficiency and connectivity of India's aviation ecosystem, which supports an estimated 370,000 direct jobs. As of December 2025, commercial engines manufactured by GE Aerospace and its partners powered the majority of commercial airline operations in India, with a fleet of more than 1,400 engines. The report states that these engines have helped Indian carriers achieve a passenger load factor of 88.2%, the highest globally, while aircraft utilisation rates have reached 12 to 14 hours per day, significantly exceeding global figures. Commenting on the announcement, Vikram Rai, CEO, South Asia, GE Aerospace, said India's commercial aviation growth was among the fastest in the world and highlighted the company's contribution beyond engine sales. He said the company's presence in India extends from component manufacturing in Pune to engineering and innovation in Bengaluru, while its partnerships with Indian customers and suppliers are helping build the next generation of the country's aerospace industry.Rai added that increasing supplier spending would strengthen the domestic supply chain and help meet growing demand as India works towards its Viksit Bharat ambitions. The report highlights the significant growth expected in India's aviation industry over the coming decades. According to Government of India estimates cited in the report, annual domestic passenger traffic is projected to reach 1.1 billion by 2040, compared with 340 million in FY26. The country's airport network is also expected to expand from 163 airports to more than 350 by 2047, creating greater demand for aircraft, engines, maintenance services and aviation infrastructure. To meet the projected demand, India and South Asia will require approximately 3,300 additional aircraft, equivalent to 6,600 additional engines, by 2044. In July 2026, IndiGo announced a memorandum of understanding with CFM International for an order of more than 1,000 LEAP-1A engines to power 510 Airbus A320neo Family aircraft. The agreement represents the largest single order ever placed for LEAP engines and a record for CFM International. It also includes support for establishing IndiGo's upcoming engine maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) facility. GE Aerospace and its partner engines are expected to power most of the approximately 1,500 new aircraft already on order with Indian carriers. The report estimates that this presents an opportunity worth more than $5.5 billion for India's MRO industry, potentially strengthening the country's position as a regional hub for aircraft engine maintenance and repair. GE Aerospace's manufacturing operations in India are centred around its flagship facility in Pune, which was established with an initial investment of $200 million. Since 2024, the company has invested nearly $55 million in expanding automation, improving precision-manufacturing capabilities and advancing workforce development at the facility. These investments have strengthened its manufacturing capabilities and supported a wider domestic supply chain comprising 17 major Indian partners, including small and medium-sized enterprises. The company's plan to nearly double supplier spending by 2030 is expected to further expand opportunities for Indian manufacturers and suppliers as demand for aircraft engines and related components increases. Workforce development remains another key area of focus. Since 2015, approximately 5,000 production associates have graduated from the Pune facility's apprenticeship programme, which enrols between 400 and 500 new apprentices every year. The programme aims to develop manufacturing skills and build a workforce capable of supporting the growing requirements of the aerospace industry.GE Aerospace also highlighted its long-standing partnership with Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL), which began in 1986 and remains an important part of India's efforts to strengthen domestic defence manufacturing. The partnership covers LM2500 naval engines and F404-IN20 engines that power India's Tejas Mk1 light combat aircraft. According to the company, the F404 platform has more than 4,000 engines deployed across 16 countries. In 2023, GE Aerospace signed a memorandum of understanding covering the potential domestic manufacture of F414 engines for the Tejas Mk2 programme. However, the proposed manufacturing arrangement remains subject to final agreements and necessary approvals. The company has also signed a five-year Performance Based Logistics contract with the Indian Air Force for Apache helicopter engines. In a separate agreement, it has committed to establishing an in-country depot facility for F404-IN20 engines. These initiatives are aimed at strengthening domestic maintenance and support capabilities, improving the availability of defence platforms and contributing to India's broader defence self-reliance objectives. GE Aerospace's Bengaluru Technology Centre, established in 2000 with an investment of $200 million, has emerged as a key centre for research, engineering and technological innovation. The facility was among the first research and engineering centres of its kind established outside the United States. Since its inception, it has secured more than 1,000 aviation patents and contributed to the design, development and certification of the GE9X engine, described by the company as the world's most powerful jet engine. Engineers at the Bengaluru centre hold key design responsibilities for the GE90, GP7200, GEnx and GE9X engines. They are also playing a significant role in the CFM RISE programme, which aims to improve fuel efficiency by 20% while meeting customer expectations for durability. The centre's Digital Technology team also supports GE Aerospace's global supply chain, MRO and sales operations through the application of artificial intelligence. In addition to its engineering work, the company is investing in the development of India's aerospace talent through academic partnerships and research programmes. These include a flagship joint innovation programme with IIT Madras, which has produced a locally designed and manufactured Micro Turbomachine. The initiative reflects the growing role of Indian engineering institutions and research centres in developing technologies for the global aerospace industry. The EY report brings together GE Aerospace's contributions across manufacturing, engineering, commercial aviation and defence over the past four decades. The company's investments in Pune and Bengaluru, its partnerships with Indian suppliers and HAL, and its workforce development initiatives form part of its strategy to expand its presence in the country. With India's aviation sector expected to grow substantially over the next two decades, the planned increase in domestic supplier spending is intended to strengthen the local manufacturing ecosystem, expand engineering capabilities and support the rising demand for aircraft engines and maintenance services. The announcement comes as India seeks to expand its aviation infrastructure, strengthen domestic manufacturing and advance its Viksit Bharat 2047 vision. GE Aerospace's proposed increase in supplier spending is expected to create further opportunities for Indian manufacturers and engineering talent while reinforcing the country's role in the global aerospace supply chain. title: Former Flipkart group employees launch petition seeking inclusion in proposed $2 billion Esop buyback
content: Synopsis On October 10, a group of former executives launched a petition aiming to bring together 20,000-30,000 former employees of Flipkart and its group companies, including Myntra, Cleartrip, Shopsy, Super Money and ANS Commerce. The petition calls for their inclusion in the planned $2 billion Esop buyback. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Agencies Former employees and executives of the Flipkart group are mobilising thousands of ex-staffers to press parent company Walmart for an exit on their vested employee stock options (Esops), as the issue gathers momentum. On October 10, a group of former executives launched a petition aiming to bring together 20,000-30,000 former employees of Flipkart and its group companies, including Myntra, Cleartrip, Shopsy, Super Money and ANS Commerce. The petition called for their inclusion in the planned $2 billion Esop buyback. The move followed an email to Walmart's board by former Flipkart group CXOs seeking a buyout of their vested options. In response, the US-based retailer's legal counsel said it will consider former employees as part of liquidity at Flipkart's initial public offering (IPO), without offering any firm commitment. Walmart has not provided a timeline for the IPO, which has stirred up a movement among former employees. âThey have said that former employees will be consideredâ¦ during the IPO when it happens,â a person familiar with the matter said on condition of anonymity. The petition said the absence of a confirmed IPO timeline could leave former employees waiting several years for a potential liquidity event. âOur options were earned through years of service, often at real personal and financial risk. We ask that the company consider former employees before the terms of the new buyback are finalised,â the petition said. The petition made three key demands: extending the exercise window for vested Esops held by former employees until the next liquidity event, ensuring they are included in the upcoming buyback on terms comparable to current employees, rather than being offered a token allocation, and appointing a point of contact to engage with a representative group of ex-staffers. The latest representation is part of a wider push by former Flipkart executives and employees for an equitable exit opportunity, with former employees raising concerns over the lack of clarity on when they would be able to monetise their vested holdings. The representation clarified that it was a request for dialogue rather than a legal notice or claim, people with knowledge of the matter said, and the signatories have asked the company to engage with their representatives before finalising the terms of the proposed buyback. Queries sent to Walmart did not elicit a response at the time of publishing. Flipkart has conducted employee liquidity programmes in the past. In July, it announced a second $50-million round under which eligible current employees could sell up to 5% of their vested stock options at a valuation of $38.2 billion. Aggrieved former staffers âMany of us gave some of the most formative years of our working lives to Flipkart, and we remain proud of what we helped build. We make this request not as a grievance, but in good faith and with continued goodwill towards the company. Our hope is simply that those who contributed to Flipkartâs journey are treated with the same fairness as those who continue it,â the petition said. Similarly, through their October 1 letter, former senior executives, including Myntra cofounder Mukesh Bansal, ex-Flipkart group chief financial officer Sanjay Baweja and chief business officer Ankit Nagori, sought âfair treatmentâ for the vested stock options that were given out 10-15 years ago. âWe contributed our time, effort, expertise and commitment to building the business and creating the value that exists today,â the letter said. âWe accepted these options as an important and integral part of our compensation and have continued to hold them for more than a decade.â Flipkartâs IPO plans, however, remain uncertain. In a July 24 interview , the companyâs group CEO Kalyan Krishnamurthy told ET, âWe don't have any timeline right now and, to be very clear, we never have had any timeline for going public. It's not a management-only decision that can be made.â The ecommerce company, which flipped its domicile back to India from Singapore in March, was preparing to tap the domestic capital markets for a public offering, according to people aware of the matter. title: Sequoia-backed chip startup Nuvacore raising funds at about a $2.5 billion valuation
content: Synopsis Nuvacore is seeking to raise the funds as the appetite for central processors has swollen due to the thirst for data-crunching capacity to power chatbots such as Anthropic's Claude. CPUs perform vital functions as traffic controllers for Nvidia's AI chips and run autonomous AI software known as agents. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters FILE PHOTO: Semiconductor chips are seen on a printed circuit board in this illustration picture taken February 17, 2023. Six-month-old microchip startup Nuvacore , which does not yet have a product, is raising hundreds of millions of dollars at a roughly $2.5 billion valuation to develop a new central processor designed for data centers , according to two people familiar with the fundraising. Nuvacore is seeking to raise the funds as the appetite for central processors has swollen due to the thirst for data-crunching capacity to power chatbots such as Anthropic's Claude. CPUs perform vital functions as traffic controllers for Nvidia's AI chips and run autonomous AI software known as agents. The roughly $2.5 billion valuation has not been previously reported. The Information reported previously that Nuvacore was raising $200 million or more. The funding round has not closed, and the people cautioned that the valuation and size of the capital raise could change. Intel and Advanced Micro Devices, which use x86 technology, have long dominated the data center CPU market. Companies designing chips based on Arm's technology - found inside Amazon and Microsoft custom CPUs - have also attempted to make inroads in the data center market. Nuvacore has not yet developed a product. Last month, it described an unconventional design strategy: to build the core functionality of the chip before committing to an architecture such as the x86 used by Intel and AMD, or Arm, which is used in most mobile phones. The design strategy will allow the company's engineers to avoid the limitations and requirements of specific architectures and optimize a design for the type of computations that are most common in data centers and AI infrastructure, Nuvacore said. Nuvacore declined to comment. The San Jose, California-based startup was founded by renowned engineers Gerard Williams , John Bruno and Ram Srinivasan. Williams, a former Apple executive, sold a prior startup called Nuvia to Qualcomm for $1.4 billion in 2021. Nuvacore earlier this year announced a seed funding round led by Sequoia Capital. It joins a series of young chip startups that have sought billion-dollar valuations before releasing a product as investor appetite for AI hardware companies has returned. Over the past decade, Silicon Valley venture capital firms have taken much less interest in hardware than software because of hardware's longer development cycles, higher capital needs and the industry's cyclical demand. Investors put about $10.7 billion into semiconductor startups in the first five months of 2026, already outpacing the $12.2 billion raised globally in all of 2025, according to Crunchbase data. Earlier this year, Intel said it could not manufacture enough chips to meet demand, and was able to sell products it had previously determined were too faulty for sale. AMD also described swelling CPU sales in a recent results conference call with analysts. Shares in both companies have risen more than 180% this year. Nvidia launched a CPU called Vera this year. CEO Jensen Huang has said the company expects to sell $20 billion worth of its Vera CPU in this fiscal year, which ends in January. Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now! title: Qualcomm and Arm jury to return next week after deliberations in contract dispute case
content: Synopsis The five-day trial that wrapped up this week was the second in two years between the companies, highlighting the deterioration of their business relationship after SoftBank Group acquired control of Arm in 2016 and Arm shifted from licensing the technology needed to make chips to selling chips of its own. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen ETtech The jury in alawsuit by chipmaker Qualcomm against chip technology supplier Arm Holdings did not reach a verdict on Friday as to whether Arm breached licensing agreements and intentionally sabotaged some of Qualcomm's dealings with Meta Platforms . The five-day trial that wrapped up this week was the second in two years between the companies, highlighting the deterioration of their business relationship after SoftBank Group acquired control of Arm in 2016 and Arm shifted from licensing the technology needed to make chips to selling chips of its own. At stake is whether Qualcomm, whose license for Arm's computing architecture runs until 2033, can eventually agree to terms for new versions of Arm's architecture. After deliberating for about four hours Friday, the jury had not reached a verdict, indicating it would return to deliberations on Tuesday. Qualcomm wants the jury to find that Arm breached its licensing agreements by withholding software patches and tools for its designs and by violating an agreement that was meant to ensure Qualcomm paid within 10% of the lowest price for Arm's processor designs. It also wants the jury to find that Arm tried to torpedo Qualcomm's dealings with Meta by leaking to Bloomberg an Arm letter in 2024 notifying Qualcomm it was allegedly in breach of a key license agreement. Arm's legal team this week tried to focus the jury on its claim that Qualcomm had not suffered any harm from the allegations in its lawsuit, which Arm cast as an attempt to exert leverage as the two fought over licensing terms. A related bench trial also took place this week over whether Arm is negotiating in good faith over those terms, though a decision on that could come well after Friday's verdict. The trial in Wilmington, Delaware, federal court hinged on many of the same episodes as the 2024 trial in which Arm failed to convince a jury that Qualcomm had breached its licensing agreement with Arm. Both trials included testimony by both Arm CEO Rene Haas and Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon and were overseen by US District Judge Maryellen Noreika. Qualcomm's lawyer Karen Dunn said in her opening statement that the case was very serious for the company. "It's really bad because Qualcomm's entire chip business depends on Arm and on Arm honoring its contract and honoring its promises," she said on Monday. Qualcomm wanted Noreika to rule prior to trial that a clause in the licensing agreements meant that Qualcomm could stop paying royalties for five years if the contract were breached. She has not issued her ruling, and Arm has argued the royalty penalty is unenforceable. "They were not harmed in the least," Arm's attorney Gregg LoCascio told the jury on Monday. title: UPI MDR framework needs rationalisation to protect public trust: Report
content: Synopsis UPI, a public digital infrastructure, has generated significant convenience for users and productivity gains for the economy, with its long-term economic benefits outweighing the incremental income that could accrue from merchant transaction fees, the report titled 'UPI at a Crossroads: Reintroducing the MDR' released by IIT Bombay said. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen IANS Proposed merchant discount rate (MDR) framework for Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transactions needs to be rationalised before implementation to protect public trust in the digital payments system , according to a report. UPI, a public digital infrastructure, has generated significant convenience for users and productivity gains for the economy, with its long-term economic benefits outweighing the incremental income that could accrue from merchant transaction fees , the report titled 'UPI at a Crossroads: Reintroducing the MDR' released by IIT Bombay said. It cautioned that public trust in UPI could be undermined if the proposed MDR framework is implemented in its present form, stressing the need to ensure that the digital payments platform does not attract negative sentiment among users. The report suggested that merchants with annual turnover of Rs 50 crore or more are mandated by law to provide UPI as a means for accepting payments. Accordingly, the remuneration for the UPI ecosystem can be harnessed by restricting it only to merchants with annual turnover of over Rs 50 crore (about 4 crore per month), it said, adding that this would account for about 90 per cent of NPCI's proposed MDR. There is a potential for NPCI to introduce a reasonable charge on merchants, within the legal mandate, across all online person-to-merchant (P2M) UPI transactions, it noted. "Such a charge imposed on e-commerce merchants , who cannot transact in cash (cash-on-delivery is more UPI-on-delivery options now), would be more in line with online merchants' digital payment facilitation fee. Such a fee can provide remuneration to all the providers of the UPI ecosystem, including banks," it said. The report argued that the proposed framework should be tweaked and rationalised to strike a balance between generating revenue to support UPI's future expansion, preserving its accessibility and acceptance among users and merchants. It also emphasised that the broader economic benefits of UPI, including productivity gains and convenience for the public, should be taken into account while framing the fee structure. As per the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) circular issued last month, a 0.4 per cent Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) will apply to person-to-merchant (P2M) UPI payments above Rs 2,000. The charge will be paid by merchants, not consumers and capped at Rs 300 for transactions of Rs 75,000 or more. Payments between individuals, as well as the vast majority of everyday merchant payments, will remain free. Essential services, such as railways, telecom, fuel, and insurance, will attract a flat Rs 5 fee per transaction above Rs 2,000. Capital markets transactions (mutual funds, stockbroking) get a lower 0.02 per cent rate, also capped at Rs 300. The NPCI, which operates the UPI platform, on September 15, issued a circular providing for MDR on certain UPI transactions, with the move aimed at creating a sustainable revenue framework for the digital payments ecosystem. The report recommended there should be no MDR on debt collection and loan EMI repayments (that may mostly be above Rs 2,000) through UPI. Keeping credit servicing and loan repayments free from MDR purview would support financial inclusion, make digital debt repayment more cost-effective than cash/cheque and prevent avoidable financial frictions for borrowers, it said. It also emphasised that the Reserve Bank should decide on MDR for UPI within the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007. Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now! title: India's quick commerce growth set to accelerate, food delivery to remain steady: Report
content: Synopsis According to the report, India's quick commerce sector is witnessing consolidation, with net order value (NOV) growth for leading platforms expected to accelerate to as much as 21.6% quarter-on-quarter in Q2FY27, as higher minimum order values and reduced discounts at some platforms shift demand towards competitors. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen ANI India's quick commerce growth set to accelerate, food delivery to remain steady: ReportÂ India's quick commerce sector is expected to see faster net order value (NOV) growth, while food delivery platforms are likely to maintain steady momentum according to an Emkay report . According to the report, India's quick commerce sector is witnessing consolidation, with net order value (NOV) growth for leading platforms expected to accelerate to as much as 21.6% quarter-on-quarter in Q2FY27 , as higher minimum order values and reduced discounts at some platforms shift demand towards competitors. "We see NOV growth of quick commerce (Qcom) companies accelerating," it said. Meanwhile, the food delivery segment is expected to maintain steady growth of around 18% year-on-year in order value. "As we step into the festive season (3Q), we expect competition to intensify," it further noted, adding, "Food Delivery should maintain momentum - ~18% NOV growth and a sustained margin trajectory." At the same time, Emkay said, India's fintech sector is expected to witness steady revenue growth and improving profitability in Q2FY27, supported by operating leverage, even as the shift in festive-season spending to the third quarter could weigh on year-on-year payment revenue growth. "Payment companies will see an impact, with the FY27 festive period shifting to 3Q vs 2Q and 3Q in FY26," it said. Meanwhile, the implementation of merchant discount rates (MDR) on UPI transactions from October 15 is expected to remain a crucial factor for the sector, it said. Under the new framework announced by the government and the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), a 0.4% merchant discount rate (MDR) will be levied from October 15 on certain UPI person-to-merchant (P2M) transactions exceeding Rs 2,000. The charge will be capped at Rs 300 for transactions of Rs 75,000 and above, while person-to-person (P2P) transfers, merchant payments up to Rs 2,000 and transactions involving eligible small merchants under the zero-MDR framework will remain exempt. According to the Emkay report, India's digital platform companies are offering attractive investment opportunities, supported by strong long-term growth potential and high operating leverage. However, it flagged differences in growth trajectories, profitability and business maturity make direct comparisons of earnings valuations difficult. "We believe that platform companies offer attractive value, considering their long growth runway and high operating leverage. Earnings multiples are not comparable across platforms, as each player has a different growth profile and operating leverage and is at a different stage of profitability," it said. title: Ecommerce firms sell goods worth Rs 24,000 crore in first two days of festive sales: Redseer
content: Synopsis Players like Amazon and Flipkart are using their quick commerce arms for sales and increasing their salience on the platform, which saw 4 to 5 times higher GMV than the BAU daily average. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Agencies à¤¤à¥à¤®à¥à¤¹à¥à¤¹à¥ à¥²à¤ªà¤µà¤°à¥à¤¨ à¤à¤¿à¤°à¤¾à¤£à¤¾ à¤®à¤¾à¤² à¤®à¤¾à¤à¤µà¤¤à¤¾à¤¯? FSSAI à¤à¥ 5 à¤®à¥à¤ à¥à¤¯à¤¾ à¤-à¤à¥à¤®à¤°à¥à¤¸ à¤ªà¥à¤²à¥ à¤à¤«à¥à¤°à¥à¤®à¥à¤¸à¤µà¤° à¤§à¤¡à¤ à¤à¤¾à¤°à¤µà¤¾à¤ E-commerce firms are estimated to have sold goods worth around Rs 24,000 crore in the first two days of the festive season sale, driven by growth in order volumes, with mobile phones accounting for the biggest share in value terms, according to consultancy firm Redseer Strategy Consultants . The consultancy firm estimated that shoppers placed about 8-9 crore orders across all platforms, including Amazon, Flipkart, Meesho , Ajio and many other marketplaces. Redseer Strategy Consultants, associate partner, Nikhil Dalal told PTI that the first two days pointed to India's festive e-commerce basket getting wider. The growth is being led by order volumes, with consumers spreading spend beyond mobiles into fashion, electronics and appliances as well. "Value fashion stood out, as shoppers from Tier-II and smaller towns bought festive wear at accessible price points. The first two days saw over $2.5 billion (close to Rs 24,200 crore) in GMV, and around 60-65 million shoppers have already participated in the first two days," he said. The growth in GMV ( gross merchandise value ) was around 6 times the business-as-usual (BAU) daily run rate, the firm said. Players like Amazon and Flipkart are using their quick commerce arms for sales and increasing their salience on the platform, which saw 4 to 5 times higher GMV than the BAU daily average. Sales of large appliances and electronics grew faster than the market, even as mobiles remained the largest category by value, according to the estimates. Mobile phones are estimated to have accounted for 38-40% or about Rs 9,100-9,600 crore of total sales. Redseer estimates consumer electronics share in total sales to be around 25-27%, or Rs 6,000-6,500 crore and fashion products in the range of 15-18%, or about Rs 3,630-4,350 crore. The 55-inch TV upgrade, large appliances and electronics together contributed approximately 25-27% of GMV. TVs, refrigerators, and ACs accounted for more than two-thirds of the large-appliance sales. Models with 55-inch screens from TCL, LG, Samsung and Xiaomi represented more than 75% of the top-selling TV SKUs. According to Redseer's estimate, electronics had already grown by more than 20% in the first half of 2026, partly as consumers brought purchases forward amid expectations of higher prices in the second half of 2026. The first two days of festive sales still recorded around 14 times more orders than average BAU, led by laptops and IoT devices in electronics. Fashion GMV grew 22-25% year-on-year in the first two days, making 15-18% share of the total GMV and about 3 to 5 times its BAU average GMV. Gen Z accounted for approximately one-third of opening-day shoppers, according to Redseer estimates. Of an estimated 6-6.5 crore shoppers who purchased during the first two days, Redseer estimates that around two-thirds of them came from Tier 2 and rural areas. Approximately 15-16 crore unique shoppers typically transact across e-commerce platforms in a business-as-usual month. "The opening two days therefore brought over one-third of this monthly shopper base into the festive sale. First-time shoppers doubled from last year. "We expect 100 million shoppers to shop in the entire 11-day first leg," Dalal said. Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now! title: India's tech push: five things to know
content: Synopsis India has committed billions of dollars in semiconductors, electronics manufacturing and artificial intelligence in a bid to become a global technology powerhouse. India's electronics production rose from about $31 billion in 2014-15 to $133 billion in 2024-25, according to the government, which wants the country to become a tech manufacturing hub. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen ANI India has committed billions of dollars in semiconductors, electronics manufacturing and artificial intelligence in a bid to become a global technology powerhouse. Prime Minister Narendra Modi said at a groundbreaking ceremony for a chip assembly and testing facility that "this decade is India's 'Techade'". But it faces a long road to match the output of rivals like the United States, China and South Korea. Here are five key things to know about India's technology push: Chips: 'national priority' From 2017-2025, India imported about $150 billion worth of microchips -- components that power everything from smartphones to weaponry. New Delhi has pledged more than $20 billion in government support to reduce that dependence. Five assembly, testing and packaging plants are now in commercial production, involving US industry titan Micron, Indian firms Kaynes, CDIL and Suchi Semicon, and CG Semi, an Indian, Japanese and Thai joint venture. But such facilities do not require the same expertise as core manufacturing and research. Another seven projects have been approved, including from Tata Electronics, which is building a chip factory in Gujarat in partnership with Taiwan's PSMC. India's semiconductor market, estimated at about $50 billion in 2026, is projected to reach $110 billion by 2030, and more than $200 billion by 2035, according to government figures. New Delhi calls building up semiconductor production "an urgent national priority". Electronics India's electronics production rose from about $31 billion in 2014-15 to $133 billion in 2024-25, according to the government, which wants the country to become a tech manufacturing hub. Global manufacturers including Apple and Samsung have expanded production in India, as companies seek to diversify supply chains beyond China. New Delhi is also trying to encourage local supply chains through incentives for component makers. Data centres India generates vast quantities of digital data but has only about three percent of global data-centre capacity, according to government figures. India believes it can provide "an alternative" to existing options, said Arvind Gupta, head of the Digital India Foundation think tank. The government says projects worth nearly $70 billion are under construction, with a further $90 billion announced. Investors include Indian conglomerates Reliance and Adani, as well as US tech giants Amazon, Microsoft and Meta. The southeastern port of Visakhapatnam is a key centre, where Google is building a $15 billion AI hub. Workforce strength The world's most populous nation says it has nearly 20 percent of the global chip-design workforce. Technology Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw says about 70,000 design engineers have been trained in the past four years. Authorities have expanded semiconductor-related courses and programmes across hundreds of engineering colleges. Modi, speaking to global technology firms at a semiconductor conference in New Delhi in September, said that "such a huge talent pool is a goldmine". But Nomura, a Japanese investment bank, calls India "ground zero" for AI-driven job disruption in Asia, given its huge workforce and vast IT-services sector. India's AI push has fuelled job-loss concerns, but the government expects AI-linked jobs to nearly double to 1.25 million by 2027. Uphill task Experts question whether India can translate ambitious plans into a competitive technology ecosystem. "India... has to navigate the complicated geopolitics of technology," Gupta said, adding it faced three key challenges. Those are "access to global capital", as well as "attracting and retaining top global talent" and "sourcing the hardware resources that are the foundation to these technologies".
