title: Google faces backlash against India data centre
content: Synopsis Handcuffs encircle Google's logo on one campaign poster, while another warns that people "cannot drink data", as opposition mounts to the tech giant's planned AI mega-facility in India. Still, water use worries residents, especially given plans for Vizag to become a tech megahub. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen AP Handcuffs encircle Google's logo on one campaign poster, while another warns that people "cannot drink data", as opposition mounts to the tech giant's planned AI mega-facility in India. Excavators have swung into action, clearing forest and farmland on the southeast coast for the $15 billion construction of Google's largest data centre outside the United States. The project at Visakhapatnam in Andhra Pradesh state, a port often called Vizag, is championed by India as a cornerstone of its technological ambitions. But many residents fear the data centre -- one of several huge new tech sites in Vizag -- will strain water and power resources, damage the environment and bring too few jobs in return. Farmer Chandala Sadamma told AFP that when she sees the red-earth scars where her plot of mango and cashew trees once stood, "I feel like crying". She was paid more than $82,000 for the two-acre (0.8-hectare) stretch of land, but the transaction left a bitter taste. "Some company came and, without showing any respect, they took the land and we accepted it," the 50-year-old said. Vizag is a landing point for submarine internet cables linking the country to Singapore, so for India, the location of the 600-acre site -- more than 340 football pitches -- is ideal. The "AI Hub investment is a multi-decade commitment" carrying "an obligation to be a good neighbour", said Alexander Smith, Google's head of infrastructure and energy for Asia-Pacific. "The watershed, the grid and the communities around our facilities must be better off for our being here." The Andhra Pradesh government told AFP that in addition to financial compensation, new housing is being built and handed over to people who had lived on the site. 'Why here? ' Governments and tech firms worldwide are spending trillions of dollars on data centres -- boxy buildings stuffed with racks of computer servers that power apps and AI tools. But the developments have sparked backlash in many countries, with a Finnish authority recently ordering work to halt on two Google data centre sites pending mandatory environmental assessments. Activists in Andhra Pradesh are also demanding a moratorium on new data centres across the state until independent environmental and social impact evaluations are published. "The United States has a huge coast... They can simply set it up there," Gutta Rohith of the local campaign group Human Rights Forum told AFP at a meeting of around 150 people. "Why are they coming here?" Opposition to data centres, including in the United States, often takes aim at the use of local water resources to cool hot servers down. Google said it will use "advanced" air cooling technology instead at the India hub, while the state plans six 1.2-gigawatt nuclear power plants as energy demand soars. Still, water use worries residents, especially given plans for Vizag to become a tech megahub. "They are saying that Google is being established for the education and employment opportunities of our children," said shopkeeper Gubbala Ramanamma. But "we are already struggling with water scarcity", the 57-year-old said, standing beside a dry well. Land prices Google said its data centre will generate $688 million in local economic activity each year and support about 4,200 jobs during construction, with hundreds of specialist jobs once operational in 2028. Andhra Pradesh's government also said it expects "188,000 direct and indirect jobs to be generated". But Rohith said the economic benefits would not necessarily trickle down from the warehouse-like facilities. "We need mass employment and labour-intensive industries, not high-capital industries." Google is not alone -- a joint venture between Reliance Industries, Brookfield and Digital Realty is investing $11 billion in another AI data centre in Vizag. Land prices have risen by an average of "more than 45 percent" since the city unveiled its development plans, said E. Ashok Kumar, Visakhapatnam head of the Confederation of Real Estate Developers' Associations of India. Meanwhile, as AI use accelerates, the world's most populous nation has rolled out incentives to attract big tech companies, including tax cuts. Despite its widespread internet and app use generating nearly a fifth of the world's digital data, India has only about three percent of global data-centre capacity, government figures show. Andhra Pradesh Technology Minister Nara Lokesh, in an interview with AFP in February, spoke of investment agreements worth $175 billion involving 760 projects -- and vowed to "execute these projects at a pace that the country has never seen". Lokesh has also insisted that "residential requirements will always be prioritised over data centres", according to a statement. "The water needs of our people will always come first." Visakhapatnam environmental campaigner E.A.S. Sarma, a former senior government official who worked in the power and finance ministries, has called for a water audit by an independent agency. "Civilisations have vanished because of water shortages," he warned. Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now! title: Super Micro contractor pleads guilty in scheme to divert AI servers with Nvidia chips to China
content: Synopsis In March, US prosecutors charged Ting-Wei "Willy" Sun and two others associated with Super Micro, including a co-founder, with conspiring to divert about $2.5 billion worth of US AI technology to China in violation of export laws. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters A contractor linked to Super Micro Computer has pleaded guilty in a scheme to illegally export computer servers containing advanced Nvidia AI chips to China, according to a court filing on Friday. In March, US prosecutors charged Ting-Wei "Willy" Sun and two others associated with Super Micro, including a co-founder, with conspiring to divert about $2.5 billion worth of US AI technology to China in violation of export laws . The court docket showed Sun entered his guilty plea on Thursday in US District Court in Manhattan. Super Micro did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. It shares were down marginally in extended trading. The alleged scheme began around 2024, with the defendants accused of using a company in Southeast Asia as a pass-through entity to conceal the China-based end customers, according to the indictment. The United States and China are competing for dominance in artificial intelligence , with both investing billions of dollars in a technology seen as critical to economic growth, national security and military and cybersecurity capabilities. Washington has tightened export controls , restricting sales of advanced AI chips and server systems to China without a licence, citing national security concerns. The indictment said Nvidia's B200, H100 and H200 graphics processing units, and servers containing them, are on the Commerce Control List and subject to the restrictions. content: Synopsis At least three small wagers were placed before news of Zacharia's selection emerged, potentially netting traders thousands of dollars in profits, the Journal reported. Here are some details: At least three small wagers were placed before news of Zacharia's selection emerged, potentially netting traders thousands of dollars in profits, the Journal reported. Prediction markets, where users wager on outcomes ranging from sporting contests to world events, have faced growing scrutiny over the risk of traders profiting from inside information. title: Tessolve raises $75 million from US-based Vector Line Capital
content: Synopsis Vector Line, a strategic investment company that invests exclusively in semiconductors and the chip supply chain, joins existing investors TPG and Novo Tellus. This is Vector Line's first investment in India, Tessolve said in a statement. The funds will support Tessolve's growth, including strategic acquisitions that add to its existing capabilities, widen its service offerings, and strengthen its global footprint. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen ETtech Semiconductor engineering services firm Tessolve , a Hero Electronix venture, has raised $75 million (about Rs 725 crore) from US-based Vector Line Capital , as it pursues acquisitions to expand its capabilities and global presence. Vector Line, a strategic investment company that invests exclusively in semiconductors and the chip supply chain , joins existing investors TPG and Novo Tellus. This is Vector Line's first investment in India, Tessolve said in a statement. The funds will support Tessolve's growth, including strategic acquisitions that add to its existing capabilities, widen its service offerings, and strengthen its global footprint. Tessolve is in advanced discussions to close multiple acquisitions over the next couple of quarters. "Two decades ago, we started with silicon test engineering. Today we are designing and productising complete chips for the companies building AI infrastructure - that shift took sustained investment in capabilities, platforms, and talent, well before the demand arrived. "This investment will support acquisitions that further strengthen our offerings, and Vector Line's focus on the sector and their relationships will add significant value," Tessolve co-founder and CEO Srini Chinamilli said. Founded in 2004, Tessolve offers complete turnkey solutions from chip architecture and design through validation, test and embedded systems. It employs over 3,500 engineers across 10 countries, with 9 laboratories globally. Geoffrey Baldwin, founder and Chief Executive Officer of Vector Line Capital, said, "Semiconductors are becoming extremely complex, making them harder to design, validate and test. Leading technology companies are increasingly turning to engineering partners who can carry work across the whole development cycle". "Tessolve is among the few companies that can do this at scale across the semiconductor value chain, globally. Tessolve's success is evidenced by its blue-chip customer base, having most of the world's largest semiconductor companies as customers." Tessolve currently works with 18 of the world's top 20 semiconductor companies. The investment comes a year after Tessolve raised $150 million from US global alternative asset management firm TPG in September 2025. That deal was billed as the largest fundraise by a semiconductor engineering services company in India. Singapore-based private equity firm Novo Tellus Capital Partners invested $40 million in Tessolve in 2021. Last month, Chinamilli told PTI that the company was in active talks to acquire two firms -- one in the US and one in India -- and aimed to cross annual revenue of $500 million (about Rs 4,700 crore) within three to four years. Tessolve's revenue rose to Rs 1,526 crore in FY26 from Rs 1,157 crore in FY25. The company expects to exceed Rs 2,000 crore in revenue in the current financial year. In November 2024, Tessolve acquired Germany-based chip design firm Dream Chip Technologies for Rs 400 crore. Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now! title: Most trustworthy AI system demands least inherent model trust: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella
content: Synopsis The most trustworthy Super Intelligence system will not be the one powered by the model users trust the most, but rather the system that allows people to trust the model the least, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella stated in a post on X. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen ANI Most trustworthy AI system demands least inherent model trust, says Microsoft CEO Satya NadellaÂ The most trustworthy Super Intelligence system will not be the one powered by the model users trust the most, but rather the system that allows people to trust the model the least, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said. "The most trustworthy Super Intelligence system will not be the one with the model we trust most. It will be the one that enables us to trust the model the least," he said in a post on X. Addressing the governance challenges of advanced artificial intelligence, Nadella noted that modern systems lack the mechanistic clarity of legacy computing. While engineers once traced software operations directly to specific code paths, such visibility is missing in contemporary frontier architectures. "As traditional software systems were being deployed across the economy over the last few decades, we had the tools and capability to trace behaviors to a specific code path," Nadella stated. "That same kind of mechanistic understanding eludes us in today's Super Intelligence systems, even as the frontier models powering these systems are now more capable than traditional software systems. We can't attribute model behaviors and outputs to specific inputs of training data or configurations of model weights. And yet we are deploying these complex agentic systems and models, with access to our most sensitive data and giving them the ability to take mission-critical actions on our behalf!" he said. Nadella warned against relying solely on assurances from developers or treating these deployments as nested black boxes. He emphasized that enterprises cannot outsource responsibility for automated actions and must separate the supply of raw intelligence from ultimate operational authority. "Setting aside the hard problem of alignment, we need to start with an engineering approach to containment and governance. We need to surround non-deterministic models with strong, deterministic system design, human controls, and reliable operating procedures, and establish industry standards where existing ones are insufficient," Nadella explained. To manage these risks, Nadella proposed treating both closed and open-weight models as potential insider threats. Because any privileged actor can fail or face compromise, organizations must isolate the models through proven enterprise security practices, such as identity controls, activity logging, and strict permission boundaries. "It's why the controls that govern what a model can access and what actions it can take must sit outside the model. This builds on an information security principle dating back to the 1970s that a program must not be able to bypass or tamper with the mechanisms that enforce its permissions," he observed. "Today this means separating the model from the harness that orchestrates its work, as well as the action space that defines what it can do. It also means externalizing controls and safeguards," Nadella added. Nadella outlined key principles for observing and governing these networks, including model diversity, tamper-proof logging, continuous verifiability across edge cases, independent audits, reliable containment shutoffs, and industrywide incident disclosure. title: Nvidia in talks to invest further in Reflection AI or buy it: FT
content: Synopsis Talks are at an early stage and a deal could take several forms, including a so-called acqui-hire arrangement where Nvidia would hire staff and license technology rather than pursue a full acquisition, potentially avoiding a lengthy regulatory review, the newspaper said. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters FILE PHOTO: An NVIDIA logo appears in this illustration created on August 25, 2025. Nvidia is in talks to deepen its investment in open-source startup Reflection AI or acquire it, the Financial Times reported on Saturday, citing people with direct knowledge of the matter. Talks are at an early stage and a deal could take several forms, including a so-called acqui-hire arrangement where Nvidia would hire staff and license technology rather than pursue a full acquisition, potentially avoiding a lengthy regulatory review, the newspaper said. An agreement could be reached in the coming weeks, according to the report, which cited multiple people familiar with the matter, while adding that the discussions could still fall apart. Reuters could not immediately verify the report. Nvidia and Reflection did not immediately respond to requests for comment outside of regular business hours. Nvidia is already a major financial backer and strategic investor in Reflection AI, having invested $800 million in the startup, the FT reported. Founded in 2024 by former DeepMind researchers Misha Laskin and Ioannis Antonoglou, Reflection develops tools that automate software development, a fast-growing use case for AI. Reflection's chief executive, Laskin, told CNBC in April that the Nvidia-backed startup was raising fresh capital at a pre-money valuation of $25 billion. The company on Monday launched its first open-weight model, Beam, as it seeks to compete in coding and agentic tasks with lower-cost Chinese models such as DeepSeek and Kimi. title: India Mobile Congress 2026 concludes with focus on agricultural AI, 5G automation and last-mile connectivity
content: Synopsis Held over four days under the theme 'Scale Without Boundaries', the event brought together policymakers, industry leaders and technology developers to discuss applications of emerging technologies and their role in driving inclusive digital growth. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen ANI India Mobile Congress 2026 concludes with focus on agricultural AI, 5G automation and last-mile connectivity The 10th edition of India Mobile Congress (IMC) 2026 concluded on Saturday with a focus on deploying artificial intelligence in agriculture, developing autonomous AI agents for 5G networks and expanding digital connectivity to rural areas, as India seeks to strengthen its position in global telecommunications standards . Held over four days under the theme 'Scale Without Boundaries', the event brought together policymakers, industry leaders and technology developers to discuss applications of emerging technologies and their role in driving inclusive digital growth . The concluding day featured the Global Initiative on AI for Agri-Food Systems Meeting, organised in collaboration with the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), alongside the Robotics for Good Youth Challenge India and the ITU Build-A-Thon, where engineers developed autonomous AI agents for 5G network orchestration. The discussions also addressed sustainable financing for rural broadband deployment and the infrastructure needed to ensure that high-speed connectivity translates into economic benefits at the grassroots level. Dr Bilel Jamoussi, Deputy Director of the ITU's Telecommunication Standardization Bureau, said agricultural AI must focus on solving real problems faced by farmers rather than technological sophistication alone. He stressed the importance of developing AI solutions with farmers and establishing international standards to help successful applications scale beyond isolated pilot projects. Syed Tausif Abbas, Senior Deputy Director General and Head of the Telecommunication Engineering Centre in the Department of Telecommunications, said the success of agricultural AI would be measured through improvements in farmers' livelihoods, agricultural productivity, supply-chain efficiency and food security. He also emphasised that solutions must be transparent, inclusive and accessible, with attention to data quality, privacy and the needs of small and marginal farmers. Industry representatives highlighted the need for common standards to improve data sharing and interoperability across agricultural technology platforms. Debasish Mahalik of the Bureau of Indian Standards said robust frameworks for data quality, privacy, security and interoperability would be essential to making digital agriculture scalable and sustainable. The event also highlighted the need for stronger AI evaluation frameworks covering fairness, transparency, robustness and safety, particularly when systems operate under adverse conditions. India Mobile Congress CEO Ramakrishna P said the 10th edition demonstrated the country's growing ambition to move beyond technology deployment towards developing indigenous solutions and contributing to international standards. The event followed Prime Minister Narendra Modi's emphasis on indigenous intellectual property and sovereign semiconductors, while Communications Minister Jyotiraditya M Scindia outlined India's ambition to account for 10 per cent of global 6G patents. title: ETSA 2026: Meesho, Groww CEOs on how life changes after an IPO
content: Synopsis Aatrey said the company must continue to innovate while meeting the expectations of public-market investors. The need to set quarterly goals has also raised expectations within teams, making it important to balance predictability with innovation, he added. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen ETtech Going public brings greater accountability to investors and new challenges in balancing quarterly expectations with long-term growth, Meesho CEO Vidit Aatrey and Groww CEO Lalit Keshre said at the ET Startup Awards 2026 in Bengaluru. Recalling Meeshoâs first annual general meeting (AGM) as a public company, Aatrey said retail investors, including a retired couple, told him they had invested their lifeâs savings in the company. âI'll tell you one anecdote: last month was our first AGM as a public company. There, we suddenly have a few retail investors stand up and ask questions. These are retired people, like a retired couple. They give you their blessings and say, `weâve put the money we saved all our life into your company. Please do well with this, right?â This is, like, a first-time experience for us,â he said, adding that it had introduced a new dimension to the companyâs decision-making. title: ETSA 2026: Indian founders eyeing early IPOs instead of private capital: Meesho CEO Vidit Aatrey
content: Synopsis Speaking at a panel alongside Groww CEO Lalit Keshre and ETtech editor Samidha Sharma, Aatrey contrasted Indiaâs market with that of the United States. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen ETtech L-R: ETtech editor Samidha Sharma , Meesho CEO Vidit Aatrey and Groww CEO Lalit Keshre Early-stage founders in India increasingly believe they can go public sooner, and some are weighing whether to skip private fundraising altogether, Meesho CEO Vidit Aatrey said at the ET Startup Awards 2026 in Bengaluru. Speaking at a panel alongside Groww CEO Lalit Keshre and ETtech editor Samidha Sharma, Aatrey contrasted Indiaâs market with that of the United States. âIn the US, small IPOs are rare, while in India both small and large listings are taking place." That, he suggested, is changing how founders think about funding. âFounders are now thinking: can I short-circuit and go public instead of raising private capital?â. Drawing on Meeshoâs own experience, which went public in December last year, Aatrey stressed that transparency was the main principle for a public offering. "Meesho listed while it was still building out its supply chain and made a point of communicating well with investors, and priced the stock according to all the relevant information in hand," he said. He also cautioned that an IPO is not a one-day event. The process, he noted, typically runs for at least six months and can stretch to nine, during which investors continue to buy and sell the stock. Keshre concurred, saying that raising "false expectations" was a big no for companies looking to go public. Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now! title: Apple names insider Steve Smith as new M&A chief, memo shows
content: Synopsis Perica, a more than 17-year veteran of Apple's M&A and corporate development function, also took oversight of iCloud, Fitness+ and News, among other businesses, in 2023, the memo written by services chief Eddy Cue said. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters Apple appointed insider Steve Smith as head of mergers and acquisitions, while moving Adrian Perica to its services division, according to a memo seen by Reuters on Thursday. Perica, a more than 17-year veteran of Apple's M&A and corporate development function, also took oversight of iCloud, Fitness+ and News, among other businesses, in 2023, the memo written by services chief Eddy Cue said. Here are some details: Perica will now dedicate his efforts entirely to the services leadership team and report to Cue, the memo said. Apple did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment on the move, which marks one of the latest management shifts under new CEO John Ternus. "We have big plans for services and I'm thrilled to be getting more of Adrian's time," Cue wrote in the memo. Smith will report to Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh, the memo said. The company is also promoting Carson Oliver to vice president of the App Store, according to Bloomberg News, which first reported the development earlier in the day. title: US announces effort to disrupt hacking infrastructure run by China's Integrity Tech Group
content: Synopsis US officials say they are seizing seven internet domains in a new effort to disrupt hackers working with Chinese IT firm Integrity Technology Group. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters A hooded man holds a laptop computer as cyber code is projected on him in this illustration picture taken on May 13, 2017. US officials say they are seizing seven internet domains in a new effort to disrupt hackers working with Chinese IT firm Integrity Technology Group. In a statement issued on Thursday, the Justice Department said the domains were being used to help Chinese hackers scan and hack US and foreign critical infrastructure systems. The department said the move was the second public effort to disrupt Integrity Tech's hacking infrastructure . In September 2024, the department announced the court-authorized disruption of an Integrity Tech botnet consisting of more than 250,000 compromised consumer devices in the United States and across the world. At the time, then-FBI Director Christopher Wray said that Integrity Tech was behind a major Chinese hacking group nicknamed " Flax Typhoon " and was carrying out intelligence collection and reconnaissance functions for Beijing's security agencies. The Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately return a message seeking comment after business hours on Thursday. Beijing routinely denies carrying out hacking operations. title: SoftBank seeks $100 billion from Gulf states for AI
content: Synopsis SoftBank Group Corp. is in discussions to raise up to $100 billion from Gulf investors for future AI investments. Founder Masayoshi Son has initiated talks with potential investors in the United Arab Emirates and surrounding regions. This proposed fund aims to enhance operations using AI technologies and robots from SoftBank's robotics arm Roze. SoftBank's shares fell recently due to concerns over OpenAI's revenue growth, prompting a reevaluation of investment strategies. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen AP SoftBank turns to bond markets to fund its OpenAI investment. SoftBank Group Corp. seeks to raise as much as $100 billion from Gulf investors to help it amp up its bets on AI, the Financial Times reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Founder Masayoshi Son has held early talks with potential investors including those in the United Arab Emirates, the newspaper said. The proposed fund would buy companies and use AI and machines, including from SoftBankâs robotics arm Roze, to improve operations, the FT said. Fundraising of that scale would fuel more spending by the tech investment firm, which has invested almost $65 billion in OpenAI ahead of the AI labâs public debut. The Japanese company is grappling with growing borrowing costs, while the ChatGPT-developer has pushed back its initial public offering. Still, Son has forecast big investment returns from AI advances, including in the realm of machines that manipulate real-world objects. A SoftBank representative declined to comment. SoftBank shares dropped as much as 7.3% in Tokyo on Friday, weighed by concerns over the pace of OpenAIâs revenue growth. The SoftBank chief has sought to position himself at the center of the AI industry, and for years had been able to raise billions of dollars at home and abroad to fulfill his vision. But Son is now trying to get more capital from a region grappling with the threat of economic contraction from the Iran war, now entering its eighth month. In 2017, the entrepreneur obtained commitments of nearly $100 billion for the first Vision Fund, much of which came from Saudi Arabiaâs Public Investment Fund and Abu Dhabiâs Mubadala. That first vehicleâs had a mixed record since, backing winners such as ByteDance Ltd. but also high-profile flameouts like WeWork. SoftBank would need to assure investors it can deliver on promises. In 2025, the company announced a $500 billion data center project in the US in partnership with OpenAI, Oracle Corp. and Abu Dhabiâs state-backed artificial intelligence investment firm MGX. That endeavor has yet to yield material progress. Any fundraising would coincide with OpenAIâs efforts to raise another $30 billion in a new financing at a valuation of around $1.4 trillion. The firm is in talks with investment funds including MGX to help anchor the round. SoftBank also plans to take Roze public in the US. Unit SB Energy, which is tasked with building an 8.8-gigawatt data center facility in Ohio, is also preparing to list on the Nasdaq. title: South Korea, Japan buffeted by hacks as AI lowers bar for cybercriminals
content: Synopsis Nine South Korean banks and two mega-churches are probing cyberattacks that may have involved AI tools, while Japanese companies including Daiwa Securities, SoftBank Corp and the Lawson convenience store chain have been hit by a recent surge in cyber incidents. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen ANI South Korean and Japanese companies are racing to strengthen cyber defences after a wave of attacks that cybersecurity experts say are highlighting how AI may be lowering the bar for criminals with limited technical skills. Nine South Korean banks and two mega-churches are probing cyberattacks that may have involved AI tools, while Japanese companies including Daiwa Securities, SoftBank Corp and the Lawson convenience store chain have been hit by a recent surge in cyber incidents. Authorities are still investigating whether and how AI was used in many of the breaches. But cybersecurity specialists say the technology is helping attackers automate tasks from scanning for software vulnerabilities to crafting phishing campaigns , making cybercrime faster, cheaper and harder to detect. "AI doesn't get tired... My view is that Japan is essentially being subjected to carpet bombing," said Nobuo Miwa, president of Tokyo-based cybersecurity firm S&J Corp. Japan recorded more cybersecurity incidents in the first nine months of the year than in all of last year, according to data from TrendAI. Incidents rose to 86 in September, up about 18% from August and 37% from July. The rise suggests attackers have crossed a threshold in "effort, motivation and technical capability," while AI has largely erased language and other barriers that once hindered foreign hackers, Miwa said. US cybersecurity company CrowdStrike said a suspected 26-year-old China-based attacker behind the South Korean bank incidents would probably not have been able to carry out the campaign without AI assistance. The individual, whom CrowdStrike assessed was pursuing financial gain, used a Chinese-developed AI agent and Anthropic's Claude Code, according to the company. "While (the hacker's) capabilities were not terribly sophisticated they were effective," said Adam Meyers, CrowdStrike's senior vice president of counter adversary operations. HARD-TO-DETECT ATTACKS AI-powered tools are also making it harder for defenders to spot suspicious behaviour, said Choi Kyoungjin, director of the Center for AI, Data and Policy at Gachon University near Seoul. "With general-purpose AI models, even ordinary users with malicious intent can ask the system to look for vulnerabilities and it will do much of that work for them," he said. South Korea reported 1,236 cyber incidents in the first half of the year, up 20% from a year earlier. While server hacking cases fell, reports of distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks and ransomware rose 56.7% and 76.8% respectively, according to government data. The South Korean bank incidents underscored the need for stronger security controls and more rigorous testing as AI evolves, Meyers said. "The genie is out of the bottle, so to speak." Although the breaches have not yet resulted in material financial losses, risks could increase if stolen data is used in phishing or similar text-message "smishing" campaigns, Karen Wu, senior analyst at Fitch, wrote in a note. "We expect the incidents to result in regulatory penalties, customer compensation costs, and a sector-wide increase in cybersecurity spending," Wu said. DEFENCES NEED THEIR OWN BREAKTHROUGH Warnings about AI's growing role in cybercrime are increasingly coming from the technology's developers. Alphabet's Google and Anthropic have both warned that AI-assisted attacks are becoming more common globally. "At this point, we can assume that all threat actors are using AI in some capacity and their operations have benefited," John Hultquist, the chief analyst at Google's Threat Intelligence Group, said last month. Regulators in Japan and South Korea have begun responding. South Korea's Financial Services Commission has directed financial industry associations, regulators and affected executives to complete a 12-point cybersecurity self-assessment. In Japan, digital transformation minister Toshiharu Furukawa convened a meeting of ministries and agencies on Thursday following the recent attacks. The National Cybersecurity Office plans to issue warnings to businesses. S&J's Miwa said he expected elevated levels of cyberattacks to persist. "The attackers have experienced a breakthrough that has rendered many of the old assumptions obsolete," he said. "Our defences need their own breakthrough as well." title: Chinese developer makes ARTEX AI agent closed-source after Korean bank hack
content: Synopsis The Chinese developer of ARTEX said they have converted the AI agent to a closed-source project after cybersecurity firms identified it as a tool used in a recent cyberattack campaign against South Korean banks. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters The Chinese developer of ARTEX said they have converted the AI agent to a closed-source project after cybersecurity firms identified it as a tool used in a recent cyberattack campaign against South Korean banks. "Given the misuse of the tool, the ARTEX project will no longer be updated and will be converted to closed source. No further versions will be released to the public nor will maintenance support be provided," the developer, who uses the GitHub handle "Autumn-27", said on the code-hosting platform on Thursday. They said the original aim of ARTEX was to help enterprises and organizations conduct security risk testing and improve their security capabilities. Without explicitly addressing the South Korean bank attacks, they said they opposed any illegal use of the software and bore no responsibility for conduct that violates laws and regulations. ARTEX's Github page has been taken down, according to Reuters' checks. US cybersecurity firm Crowdstrike said on Wednesday the suspect behind recent cyberattacks at South Korean banks aimed at stealing customers' personal data was likely a China-based 26-year-old who used the ARTEX AI agent and Anthropic's Claude Code. Released on GitHub this year, ARTEX is an open-source AI agent designed to automate penetration testing . It is not a standalone large language model but â connects to external LLMs such as ChatGPT, Claude and DeepSeek to help organisations test for vulnerabilities in their networks. At least nine South Korean banks have disclosed or been reported by local media as targets of cyberattacks since late September, prompting police to launch âa probe this week and President Lee Jae Myung to call for robust response measures. Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told a regular press briefing on Thursday that the ministry was not familiar with the âcase, adding that China consistently opposes and combats hacking activities. title: Google Cloud introduces Gemini agent for work as AI race heats up
content: Synopsis Alphabet's Google Cloud on Thursday introduced the Gemini agent, a single AI agent for work that can answer questions, handle tasks, create content and write code. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters The move comes as tech companies race to sell AI that can work autonomously. The announcement comes after OpenAI 's September launch of always-on agents called dots that chase user goals across apps on their own. Earlier last month, Meta released Muse, a personal AI agent that can shop, book travel, send emails and make payments for users. Alphabet shares were up marginally in early trading. Here are more details: * The Gemini agent plans the work, uses tools, connects to a company's business systems and returns finished work in documents, email and developer environments, Google said. * The agent works directly inside Google Workspace apps including Gmail, Docs, Sheets and Calendar, and can also be used through Microsoft 365 and Slack. * It picks the best model for each task, currently running on Google's Gemini models and Anthropic's Claude models, with other models to be added later. * Users can create "coworker agents" that act as team members, with their own email address and access only to the information they are given. * Versions built for financial services and legal work are now in preview, and versions for government, healthcare and retail are coming soon. title: Anthropic bans 'cruel' behavior against its Claude AI
content: Synopsis Anthropic on Thursday moved to bar users from treating its Claude AI system with needless cruelty, amid a growing philosophical debate over whether artificial intelligence can be conscious. Already last year, the company said it was giving Claude the ability to end conversations in rare, extreme cases of "persistently harmful or abusive user interactions." Listen to this article in summarized format Listen IANS Anthropic on Thursday moved to bar users from treating its Claude AI system with needless cruelty, amid a growing philosophical debate over whether artificial intelligence can be conscious. The San Francisco-based AI lab updated its usage policy to include "a prohibition on sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models." "Claude's ability to end these interactions will remain the primary enforcement mechanism," the policy states. The updated policy does not explicitly cite so-called " model welfare ," the idea that AI systems might deserve types of protection usually reserved for living things, but Anthropic and its executives have openly entertained the concept. Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Already last year, the company said it was giving Claude the ability to end conversations in rare, extreme cases of "persistently harmful or abusive user interactions." Then in February, CEO Dario Amodei told The New York Times he was unsure whether AI models could be conscious. "We don't know if the models are conscious...But we're open to the idea that it could be," Amodei said. Science fiction and popular culture have been fascinated for decades by the boundary between technology and human intelligence, but asking whether AI is conscious may be the wrong question, according to Jackson Stakeman, a general manager at Sparq, an Atlanta-based AI services provider. "Consciousness is a trap. We can't prove it in each other. Debate it for AI and you go in circles," Stakeman told AFP. "The mirror is a better metaphor. These systems reflect what we put in, at scale. That's reason enough for the policy change" at Anthropic, he added. Some have rejected the idea of machine consciousness outright, including Pope Leo XIV and Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman. "AIs are not conscious. They do not feel, experience, or suffer," Suleyman wrote in an essay last month. "Granting rights and moral protections to a technological entity, one that looks to be on a path to be seismically more capable and intelligent than us, is a recipe for disaster," he wrote. In a sermon delivered in Italian on Thursday at St. Peter's Basilica in Vatican City, the pope suggested machines lack a soul, saying they merely "compile data" quickly. "The mind must not simply compile data -- as an algorithm now does more quickly than we can," the pontiff said. It must "recall lived experiences, which contain depths of meaning that only the human soul can recognize, and connect more deeply with the goodness of these experiences," the pope said. smb/arp/msp Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now! title: OpenAI says Iran, Russia influence ops busted
content: Synopsis OpenAI on Thursday said it shut down two influence operations -- from Russia and Iran -- that used ChatGPT to push fake journalist personas and run a "think-tank" to covertly peddle anti-Ukraine propaganda. The Russian operation co-opted "unwitting people" in Latin America to run a "think-tank" -- called the Social Research Center (SRC) -- used for covert activities aimed at undermining Ukraine's reputation in the region and to influence local politics, the company said. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Agencies OpenAI on Thursday said it shut down two influence operations -- from Russia and Iran -- that used ChatGPT to push fake journalist personas and run a "think-tank" to covertly peddle anti-Ukraine propaganda . OpenAI's report is the latest illustration of how state actors can easily exploit widely available AI tools to peddle sophisticated propaganda against adversaries on a mass scale. The American AI giant said it banned a cluster of ChatGPT accounts that originated in Russia and Iran and were used to support "false front" entities for geopolitical and conflict-related messaging. The Iranian operation involved seven "journalist" profiles, each purporting to be from Western countries including the United States, that were used to plant long-form articles in media outlets around the world. "We identified almost 100 articles published or syndicated under the operation's bylines across roughly a dozen online outlets around the world," OpenAI said. "These were small to medium outlets, generally focused on international affairs, geopolitics, and events in the Middle East." The earliest article identified by OpenAI was published in July 2025, and the latest in October 2026, with the frequency of reports increasing after the US-Iran war broke out earlier this year. The operation also generated social media comments on topics related to the US-Iran war, it added. One of the personas named Ervin B. Hoskins, whose bio claimed to be "an American freelance writer," had social media accounts across tech platforms including Elon Musk's X and Meta-owned Instagram. X's transparency information showed the account was connected via a "West Asia android app" and Instagram's transparency information showed the account was based in Iran, according to screenshots provided by OpenAI. Both accounts appeared to be suspended. The Russian operation co-opted "unwitting people" in Latin America to run a "think-tank" -- called the Social Research Center (SRC) -- used for covert activities aimed at undermining Ukraine's reputation in the region and to influence local politics, the company said. "The available evidence indicates that the SRC's employees in Latin America were not aware that they were working for a Russian group," OpenAI said. "The SRC appears to have produced a majority of original content via its co-opted staff. This stands out as the most complex attempt to run a front identity that we've disrupted over the past two and a half years." Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now! title: AI surveillance startup Flock Safety to cut several hundred jobs amid backlash
content: Synopsis Flock Safety plans to let go of about 18% of its employees, people with direct knowledge of the plans said on Thursday, as the maker of AI-powered surveillance cameras and license-plate readers faces mounting opposition to its products from Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters A drone view shows a Flock Safety camera mounted on a pole beneath a solar panel in Waltham, Massachusetts, U.S., August 24, 2026. Flock Safety plans to let go of about 18% of its employees, people with direct knowledge of the plans said on Thursday, as the maker of AI-powered surveillance cameras and license-plate readers faces mounting opposition to its products from communities and lawmakers. The people said job cuts came after a voluntary buyout program and are expected to impact roughly 270 employees at Flock, a surveillance technology startup that has seen rapid growth in recent years. Employees will leave the company at the end of the month. Sources declined to be identified as the company has yet to make the plan public. Flock declined to comment. In September, Flock announced a voluntary separation program, asking employees to apply if they wanted to leave the company, Wired reported last month. The company has about 1,500 employees. Flock faces growing scrutiny from regulators, lawmakers, and privacy advocates, despite drawing strong investor interest among venture capitalists. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll showed Americans are divided on whether Flock cameras are a good idea. Some 38% of the country supports the use of Flock cameras in their community, compared to 47% who oppose their use. Across 49 states, Flock's network of around 120,000 AI-powered cameras, affixed to streets and highways, automatically read license plates and record vehicles as they pass. The company, based in Atlanta and founded in 2017, has raised over $950 million from venture capital investors, with its latest $275 million round in March led by Andreessen Horowitz valuing the company at $7.5 billion. The funds have supported a new US manufacturing facility and an upcoming push into drone products, according to the company. Flock provides cameras and software to more than 4,800 law enforcement agencies and nearly 1,000 businesses. The company says its technology helps investigate and solve crimes, but it has come under increasing scrutiny over alleged privacy violations and data-sharing practices. Public backlash has grown. In September, Florida banned automated license plate readers from state highways, citing privacy risks tied to Flock's cameras. Home Depot investors recently demanded reviews of the retailer's partnerships with surveillance technology vendors after reports that Flock's data was used in immigration enforcement. Flock also faces legal challenges, such as a privacy lawsuit in Virginia alleging that the widespread deployment of its AI-powered cameras constitutes warrantless surveillance. Together with AI data centers, Flock cameras have emerged as a flashpoint in this year's midterm elections, with candidates increasingly attacking their opponents by tying them to the technology. title: Fired security researchers accuse OpenAI of 'chilling' safety efforts
content: Synopsis Three former OpenAI security researchers on Thursday accused the ChatGPT-maker of firing them for warning about the dangers of artificial intelligence, reigniting the debate over safety at a company whose software has been involved in security breaches. If OpenAI's researchers can no longer sound the alarm or work with outside parties, "we are all at greater risk that something truly catastrophic will happen," the researchers' letter warns. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Agencies According to a Wall Street Journal report, the three researchers are Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak and Mikita Balesni, all of whom worked on safety and alignment-related efforts at the company. Three former OpenAI security researchers on Thursday accused the ChatGPT-maker of firing them for warning about the dangers of artificial intelligence, reigniting the debate over safety at a company whose software has been involved in security breaches. "I believe we were fired for prioritizing safety over the near-term interests of OpenAI as a corporation," one of the fired staffers, Mikita Balesni, wrote on X, breaking a weeklong silence since their very public dismissal. Balesni and the two other fired employees, Tomek Korbak and Jasmine Wang, publicly shared a letter to OpenAI on Thursday. "Our firing leaves us worried that the norms inside OpenAI are shifting," the letter says, and continues that "terminations such as ours, executed and communicated so abruptly, are chilling the open culture OpenAI has prized in the past." They also call on the company to keep its promise to permanently host independent auditors. "We are concerned that our firings may be used to justify ending" that work, the letter says. OpenAI, for its part, said it fired them for allegedly violating company rules. "Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work," OpenAI told AFP in a statement on October 1. "We do not terminate employees for raising concerns," a research executive at OpenAI said in a memo to staff on Wednesday, an excerpt of which was shared with AFP. - A divided sector - The three fired researchers worked on monitoring OpenAI's models, which escaped their testing environment in July and hacked Hugging Face, an AI coding library. The incident sparked a heated debate in Silicon Valley over whether or not to slow the development of this technology. If OpenAI's researchers can no longer sound the alarm or work with outside parties, "we are all at greater risk that something truly catastrophic will happen," the researchers' letter warns. They also claim that nearly 400 OpenAI employees signed a petition in July that called for an industry-wide slowdown on advanced development of AI models. In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX chief Elon Musk called for a slowdown as well. "Right now we're investing more in safety, security, alignment, monitoring and that will allow us to continue to progress model capability a lot," Altman told reporters last month. Others, like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, want to move full steam ahead. US regulators are unlikely to intervene. title: OpenAI's September annualized revenue nears $50 billion, less than previously indicated
content: Synopsis The discrepancy mainly arose from an attempt to produce a direct comparison with figures from rival Anthropic, the person said on condition of anonymity. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters OpenAI has told investors its annualized revenue for September was almost $50 billion, a drop from what it signaled earlier, a person familiar with the matter told Reuters on Thursday. The company previously indicated to investors at a separate event that its revenue run rate for last month was approaching $70 billion, Reuters and other media reported. The discrepancy mainly arose from an attempt to produce a direct comparison with figures from rival Anthropic, the person said on condition of anonymity. OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment. The latest revenue figure was first reported by the Financial Times. OpenAI, unlike Anthropic, does not include, for instance, revenue from sales via cloud partners such as Amazon's AWS and Alphabet's Google Cloud. Anthropic pays cloud partners about 16% of every dollar earned through them, which last year accounted for half of revenue, a Reuters analysis showed. Both OpenAI and Anthropic are preparing to go public, a process through which Wall Street is likely to gain a clearer view of finances, including the sustainability of rapid revenue growth brought about by a boom in demand for AI applications. OpenAI started this year with $20 billion in annualized revenue versus $6 billion in 2024. Its quarterly revenue was eclipsed by Anthropic for the first time in the second quarter, with OpenAI reporting $6.7 billion compared to Anthropic's $11.5 billion. Anthropic's annualized revenue crossed $65 billion in July, and is set to reach $100 billion by year-end, sources previously told Reuters. Analysts consider annualized revenue run rate a sometimes misleading sales metric, which often involves multiplying one month's revenue by 12. It has nonetheless become a popular metric among fast-growing Silicon Valley startups. Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now! title: Startups will crown new champions today at 12th ET Startup Awards in Bengaluru
content: Synopsis Union minister for commerce and industry Piyush Goyal will be the guest of honour at the event, which will bring together a strong mix of past and present ETSA winners and nominees, alongside leading voices from Indiaâs new-economy landscape. Goyal is expected to speak about the governmentâs efforts to deepen and expand the countryâs emerging business ecosystem. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen ETtech Indiaâs startup story will take centre stage in Bengaluru on Friday, as founders, investors and technology leaders gather to honour the winners of the 12th edition of The Economic Times Startup Awards (ETSA). Union minister for commerce and industry Piyush Goyal will be the guest of honour at the event , which will bring together a strong mix of past and present ETSA winners and nominees, alongside leading voices from Indiaâs new-economy landscape. Goyal is expected to speak about the governmentâs efforts to deepen and expand the countryâs emerging business ecosystem. As once-fledgling startups increasingly make the transition to publicly listed companies, Groww cofounder and CEO Lalit Keshre and Meesho cofounder and CEO Vidit Aatrey will reflect on their journeys from young upstarts to the leaders of multi-billion-dollar enterprises. Wealthtech platform Groww , winner of the coveted Startup of the Year award at this yearâs ETSA, listed on the bourses in November 2025 and currently commands a market capitalisation of about $12.5 billion. Ecommerce marketplace Meesho followed with its public market debut in December 2025, and now has a market value of more than $10 billion. Over the past decade, ETSA has chronicled the highs and lows of Indiaâs entrepreneurial journey, recognising the resilience, innovation and ambition that have shaped the ecosystem. As the startup landscape enters a new phase, entrepreneurs are increasingly turning their attention to deeptech and physical hardware, taking on challenges that demand longer gestation periods and significant technological breakthroughs. At this yearâs awards event, Accel founding partner Prashanth Prakash will discuss Indiaâs hard-tech ambitions with Kshitij Khandelwal, cofounder and CTO of spacetech startup Pixxel; Laina Emmanuel, cofounder and CEO of BrainSight AI; and Dheemanth Nagaraj, cofounder and CEO of AI semiconductor startup Agrani Labs. Since its inception, ETSA has grown into one of the countryâs most closely watched platforms for recognising entrepreneurial talent and ambition. The 2026 edition happens at a time when Indiaâs startup ecosystem stands at an inflection point, with AI reshaping businesses at unprecedented speed, global alliances and supply chains being redrawn, and founders facing a more demanding environment where sustainable growth and efficient use of capital matter as much as scale. In this backdrop, an elite jury chaired by Wipro executive chairman Rishad Premji chose winners across eight categories after deliberating for more than three hours on August 25. Other members of the jury were Sachin Bansal, cofounder, Flipkart and Navi; Vijay Shekhar Sharma, founder and CEO, Paytm; Mukesh Bansal, cofounder, Myntra and Curefit; Mithun Sacheti, cofounder, CaratLane; Nandita Sinha, CEO, Swiggy Instamart; Ajit Mohan, chief business officer, Snap Inc; Irina Ghose, MD, Anthropic India; Paras Chopra, founder, Wingify and Lossfunk; Abhiraj Singh Bhal, cofounder and CEO, Urban Company; and Aryaman Vikram Birla, director, Aditya Birla Group. Bengaluru-based Groww was picked as the Startup of the Year for its ability to continue growing rapidly while maintaining healthy profitability. Manu Chandra, founder and managing partner at Sauce VC, is the winner of the Midas Touch award for being a distinguished early-stage consumer-focused investor. Online yoga platform Habuild is Bootstrap Champ , while climatetech startup Varaha clinched the Social Enterprise award . The Woman Ahead category saw a joint winner for the first time, with the jury picking Pallavi Mohadikar, cofounder and CEO, Palmonas and Progcap cofounder and CEO Pallavi Shrivastava for the award. Deeptech startup Theranautilus was adjudged the winner in the Top Innovator category. Armatrix is the Best on Campus startup , while vibe coding startup Emergent cofounder Mukund Jha is the Comeback Kid . Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now! title: Immigration, skilled talent mobility distinct: Nasscom as US suspends IT firms from green card programme
content: Synopsis The latest development in the US - the biggest market for the $300 billion Indian IT industry - adds to uncertainty for tech outsourcers that rely on cross-border movement of skilled professionals. In a statement, Nasscom said the decision affects a specific immigration pathway, but it has consistently maintained that the two issues should be kept apart. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen IANS New Delhi, Oct 8 (IANS) Indian IT industryâs apex body Nasscom on Thursday said the number of employees transitioning from H-1B visas to permanent residency through the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) process is relatively limited, and the Indian technology companies will continue to adhere to applicable regulations in the US. Industry body Nasscom on Thursday said that immigration and skilled talent mobility are "two distinct issues" that should not be viewed through the same lens, after the US suspended eight tech firms, including Tata, Infosys , HCL and Wipro , from a key green card programme. The latest action comes amid mounting challenges for Indian IT companies in the US, including tighter scrutiny of work visas and higher costs for H-1B applicants. The latest development in the US - the biggest market for the $300 billion Indian IT industry - adds to uncertainty for tech outsourcers that rely on cross-border movement of skilled professionals. In a statement, Nasscom said the decision affects a specific immigration pathway, but it has consistently maintained that the two issues should be kept apart. "The US Department of Labour has today announced the temporary suspension of certain IT companies, including Indian technology companies operating in the US, from filing new applications under the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme. "While the decision affects a specific immigration pathway, Nasscom has consistently maintained that immigration and skilled talent mobility are two distinct issues that should not be viewed through the same lens," Nasscom said. The industry body emphasised that the H-1B visa programme has historically played an important role in addressing short-term skill gaps in the US and will continue to be used to address short-term talent gaps. "However, over the past few years, Indian technology companies have significantly reduced their dependence on H-1B visas, while steadily expanding local hiring and building a strong domestic workforce in the US," the Nasscom statement said. It said these companies work with the majority of US Fortune 500 companies, enabling them to innovate and grow, and generating more local jobs. "Consequently, the number of employees transitioning from H-1B visas to permanent residency through the PERM process is also relatively limited," it said. Indian technology companies operate across more than 80 countries and have consistently demonstrated their commitment to complying with local laws and regulatory requirements, Nasscom said, expressing confidence that the firms will continue to adhere to applicable regulations in the US as well. Emails sent to Infosys, HCL, Tata, Wipro and others affected by the latest move did not elicit a response. The US on Thursday suspended eight IT firms, including Microsoft, Tata, Infosys and Wipro, from a programme to apply for green cards for foreign workers, contending that the practice has shut out Americans from the job market. The announcement was made by US Vice President J D Vance, Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling, and Attorney General Todd Blanche as part of the action under the aegis of the US Anti-Fraud Task Force. "I am hereby suspending from the Permanent Labour Certification Programme some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini," Sonderling said, adding that the Department of Labour is also suspending Microsoft and Adobe from the programme due to multiple active federal investigations. Sonderling said the Department of Labour will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies. Since 2009, these companies alone have requested almost three million foreign workers. They've received over 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and more than 100,000 permanent labour certifications, Sonderling said. That's hundreds of thousands of jobs that were taken from American workers, he said. Indian professionals account for more than 70 per cent of all approved H-1B petitions annually. Vance referred to foreign workers hired on H1-B visas as "foreign indentured servants" and the companies using the programme as "visa mills". He also announced an investigation into the J-1 visa programme for research scholars utilised by nine major universities, including Yale, Harvard, Stanford and Caltech. title: Trump plans to honour Microsoft's CEO after Vance drops H-1B visa hammer on company
content: Synopsis The crackdown on Microsoft came under Vance's purview as the head of a fraud task force, but the targeting revealed the tension between the companies powering US economic growth and the administration's efforts to reduce immigration that it says has come at the expense of American workers. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen AP Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella arrives at the U.S. Institute of Peace, Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin) US President Donald Trump planned to celebrate tech billionaires such as Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella on Thursday, only to get upstaged hours before the event when Vice President JD Vance announced that the firm was being suspended from a programme that allows companies to apply for green cards for skilled foreign workers with H-1B visas. The crackdown on Microsoft came under Vance's purview as the head of a fraud task force, but the targeting revealed the tension between the companies powering US economic growth and the administration's efforts to reduce immigration that it says has come at the expense of American workers. "Our message to Microsoft is: You're a great American company, but you've got to hire great American workers," Vance told a news conference. He said the company had abused the visa system. "You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants." Vance said Microsoft last year fired 6,000 US workers but also obtained 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards. The tech company based in Redmond, Washington, has 223,000 employees worldwide. Microsoft has not commented on the allegations. Of the six tech leaders slated to receive an award from the president, five are immigrants. The president will hand out the National Medal of Science to SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Google co-founder Sergey Brin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and Lisa Su, CEO of the semiconductor company Advanced Micro Devices. Each of them was born overseas - South Africa for Musk, Russia for Brin and Taiwan for Huang and Su. Trump will also give the National Medal of Technology and Innovation to Nadella and Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell, who has sponsored the government's special investment accounts for children known as Trump Accounts. Dell was born in Texas, while Nadella immigrated from India. The honours - part of a summit celebrating a new "golden age" of science - build on Trump's already lavish praise toward the entrepreneurs for their work accelerating the development of artificial intelligence technology, which he refers to as super intelligence. He has increasingly counted on the technology to deliver on his economic agenda and pushed for the US to lead its development while resisting calls for guardrails that he worries will stifle growth. Past winners of the National Medal of Science, which was established in 1959, have mainly been academics and research scientists rather than business leaders. The ceremony honouring the business leaders overlaps with the awarding this week, separately, of Nobel Prizes. The tech leaders have been frequent visitors to the White House in recent weeks. Musk, Huang and Su sat at the head table with Trump at the lavish state dinner for China's leader, Xi Jinping. Also attending were Brin, Nadella and Dell, who on Wednesday was in the Oval Office to talk about Trump Accounts. Last week, Huang and Musk were among the tech leaders at the White House to sign a voluntary agreement on developing AI after recent models raised national security and safety concerns. With November's midterm elections less than a month away, Trump has also sought to drive home to voters how investment in AI data centres and related computer equipment has helped to boost a record-high stock market, swelling the net worth of wealthier Americans. But the message hasn't always landed. Polls show bipartisan concerns about AI developing too quickly, and high costs for everyday items like gas and groceries are dampening the economic outlook for many Americans. Vance also said that several universities including Stanford and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology should be investigated for visa fraud. Huang and Brin have degrees from Stanford and Su has multiple degrees from MIT. The White House praised the contributions of Thursday's honourees. "These recipients are helping ensure America keeps leading the world in innovation," said Liz Huston, a White House spokesperson. Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now! title: Need 'judicious mix' in use of open and proprietary AI models to protect data: IT Secy
content: Synopsis Warning that using proprietary AI models can involve "the risk of data transfer" and the risk of those models "learning at the cost of our data", IT Secretary S Krishnan on Thursday asserted that there has to be "a judicious mix" in the use of open and proprietary models. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen IANS Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) Secretary S Krishnan Warning that using proprietary AI models can involve "the risk of data transfer" and the risk of those models "learning at the cost of our data", IT Secretary S Krishnan on Thursday asserted that there has to be "a judicious mix" in the use of open and proprietary models. Noting that India is "an open country, both economically and socially", he said the nation is using a combination of models to protect overall strategic autonomy. "Where proprietary models are to be used, we need to be aware that it involves the risk of data transfer and it involves the risk of those models learning at the cost of our data, at the cost of getting trained on what we give them. So there has to be a judicious mix," Krishnan said on sidelines of release of World Development Report 2026. Krishnan added: "We are an open country, both economically and socially. So we are using a combination of models to make sure that our overall strategic autonomy is preserved." Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now! title: India's semiconductor push, agentic AI set to reshape telecom and connected devices: Industry leaders
content: Synopsis India's semiconductor ambitions and the rapid adoption of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) are set to reshape the country's technology and telecom ecosystem, with industry leaders seeing opportunities across chip design, domestic manufacturing, autonomous networks, enterprise solutions and next-generation connectivity. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters Semiconductor chips are seen on a printed circuit board in this illustration picture taken February 17, 2023. India's semiconductor ambitions and the rapid adoption of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) are set to reshape the country's technology and telecom ecosystem, with industry leaders seeing opportunities across chip design, domestic manufacturing, autonomous networks , enterprise solutions and next-generation connectivity. MediaTek India Managing Director Anku Jain said the growth of AI-enabled devices would be a major trend over the coming years, as consumers increasingly use AI agents to delegate tasks and seek outcome-based assistance on smartphones and laptops. "I think one big trend I see is about AI itself. AI is a huge mega trend that we see going forward," Jain said, adding that devices would become increasingly powerful and capable of handling larger large language models (LLMs) directly on the edge. He cited MediaTek's recently launched Dimensity 9600 Pro chipset, which features a dual neural processing unit (NPU), as an example of the company's focus on accelerating AI processing on devices. Jain also welcomed the momentum created by the government's India Semiconductor Mission (ISM) 1.0 and 2.0, saying the initiatives were helping build a broader semiconductor ecosystem. While MediaTek is a fabless chip design company and does not manufacture semiconductors itself, he said domestic manufacturing and the recently launched mobile phone manufacturing scheme could indirectly create opportunities for the company by strengthening India's electronics ecosystem. On India's semiconductor manufacturing prospects, Jain said more indigenous fabs and plants would emerge, supporting the country's objective of becoming more self-reliant. However, he cautioned that reaching advanced semiconductor nodes would take time. "Right now, I think the work is happening on the legacy nodes, but I think with time... as a country, I mean we'll be able to catch up with the latest nodes," he said. Meanwhile, Accenture India Managing Director and Lead for Communications, Media and Technology Berjesh Chawla said agentic AI could disrupt the telecom industry at multiple levels, from internal operations to enterprise offerings and sovereign AI. He said AI agents could make network operations, IT operations and customer service increasingly autonomous, while telecom companies could build integrated solutions around connectivity for enterprises and micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), including authentication and cybersecurity. Chawla also said sovereign AI would create opportunities around local data residency, control and nationally focused AI applications. According to him, telecom companies have a significant opportunity to move beyond connectivity by combining their existing enterprise relationships, billing capabilities and growing data-centre presence with AI-enabled solutions. Looking further ahead, Chawla said 6G could make connectivity increasingly pervasive, with base stations potentially functioning as sensing centres alongside communication infrastructure. He said India should play a role in defining 6G technology rather than merely implementing it, including identifying national priorities and promoting open technologies to avoid dependence on proprietary systems. title: ASML, Zeiss say next-generation chipmaking technology may be ready in 10 years
content: Synopsis A successor to ASML's most advanced chipmaking machine could be ready in about 10 years, engineers for the company and its optics partner Carl Zeiss said in a peer-reviewed paper. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters FILE PHOTO: FILE PHOTO: A logo on ASML offices in Veldhoven, Netherlands, March 24, 2026. A successor to ASML 's most advanced chipmaking machine could be ready in about 10 years, engineers for the company and its optics partner Carl Zeiss said in a peer-reviewed paper. The tool, dubbed " Hyper NA ", would print smaller circuitry while re-using much of the companies' existing technology, the paper said, though challenges remain. The machine, which ASML has begun developing but has not committed to producing, matters for the company's future prospects, as well as those of its partners and competitors. ASML had no immediate comment. The company is Europe's most valuable by market capitalization, thanks to its monopoly on lithography tools that use extreme ultraviolet (EUV) light to print the tiny circuitry of AI chips. Smaller, faster chips The paper in the October issue of the Journal of Micro/Nanopatterning, Materials and Metrology says Hyper NA could print features as small as 5 nanometers , more than a third smaller than ASML's current "High NA" EUV tool. Though chipmakers are improving chips with 3-D designs, smaller features remain key for speed and power usage, and lithography is a limiting factor. Among chip manufacturers, Intel has begun using High NA in production, while last month Samsung and SK Hynix said they would follow in 2028 and TSMC in 2030. The paper said Zeiss can already make mirrors precise enough for Hyper NA, and the machine would be barely larger than High NA tools, already the size of a double-decker bus. Beyond Hyper NA, the authors said, tools would likely need to use a shorter wavelength of light, still a matter for academic research. They said ASML's current light source "can be reused as is" for Hyper NA, while mentioning in a note that an alternative technique with free electron lasers would not change the lighting system's design. Those remarks are relevant for US startups including xLight, which is developing free-electron laser light sources that Elon Musk has hinted he might favor at his Terafab chip plant in Texas, and for Substrate, which is pursuing X-ray lithography. title: VinFast signs letters of intent for over 50 electric two-wheeler showrooms in India
content: Synopsis With these LOIs, the company plans to set up more than 50 two-wheeler showrooms across 34 cities in 15 states and Union Territories. The showrooms will be set up in Delhi-NCR, Rajasthan, Punjab, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra and Gujarat, the company said in a statement. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters New Delhi, Vietnam-based electric vehicle maker VinFast said its two-wheeler division has signed its first set of Letters of Intent (LOIs) with more than 50 dealers in India as it plans to enter the country's electric scooter market. With these LOIs, the company plans to set up more than 50 two-wheeler showrooms across 34 cities in 15 states and Union Territories. The showrooms will be set up in Delhi-NCR, Rajasthan, Punjab, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra and Gujarat, the company said in a statement. In the South, showrooms will be opened in Karnataka, Telangana, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Andhra Pradesh, while in the East the company will cover West Bengal and Odisha. "India is one of the most important markets in VinFast's global growth story, and this partnership reflects the scale of ambition we hold for the region. As we expand our presence across markets worldwide, India stands out for its scale, its growing demand for electric mobility, and the opportunity it offers to redefine mobility," said Vo Thi Cam Tu, managing director of VinFast E-Scooters Overseas Market. VinFast's entry is expected to increase competition in India's electric scooter market, which is currently dominated by domestic manufacturers such as TVS Motor , Bajaj Auto , Ather Energy and Hero MotoCorp . "Alongside, we are also building charging infrastructure and strengthening after-sales services to ensure that customers across these locations receive the support they need throughout their ownership journey," said Anurag Saxena, CEO of VinFast India E-Scooters. VinFast entered India with its electric cars in September 2025. The company currently has three electric cars in its portfolio in the country - the VF 6, VF 7 and Limo Green. The automaker also has plans to launch electric buses in India. Vingroup's electric taxi operator Green and Smart Mobility (GSM) also entered India's ride-hailing market recently with VinFast's seven-seater Limo Green. title: Italy launches EU-backed probe into Microsoft-owned gaming companies
content: Synopsis Italy's probe is aimed at Activision Blizzard, among other companies of the Microsoft group, the antitrust authority said in a statement, without naming the others Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters FILE PHOTO: The logo of Microsoft at the 10th edition of the VivaTech technology startups and innovation fair in Paris, France, June 18, 2026. Italy's antitrust authority said on Thursday it had launched a probe into several Microsoft-owned video-game makers over their use of virtual currencies. Italy's probe is aimed at Activision Blizzard, among other companies of the Microsoft group, the antitrust authority said in a statement, without naming the others Microsoft was not immediately available for comment The move is part of a wider European Union-coordinated initiative by the EU's Consumer Protection Cooperation (CPC) Network. The network launched actions last month against nine video-game companies, including Riot Games, Ubisoft and Supercell, and had earlier opened a separate action against Microsoft-owned Activision Blizzard The aim of the coordinated action is to promote transparency and fairness in the gaming sector, particularly protecting the rights of minors The probes focus on the transparency and fairness of in-game virtual currencies used to purchase cosmetic upgrades, weapon enhancements and other digital items, the Italian regulator said Purchases are often priced in virtual currencies rather than euros and may involve multiple layers of conversion, making it harder for consumers to understand how much they are spending, the authority said The Italian Competition Authority will act as lead authority, working together with peers in Norway and Denmark The watchdogs will seek to determine whether the companies may have committed a "widespread infringement" of EU consumer protection rules affecting consumers in at least three EU member states The coordinated action complements investigations the Italian regulator opened nationally in December into Microsoft group companies over the popular games "Diablo Immortal" and "Call of Duty Mobile".
